In fact, inequality and marginalization are usually at interface in that they both with interacts and reinforces each other. Religious minority groups are amongst those who encounter severe exclusion, discrimination and oppression. In case of Indian Muslims as a religious marginalized community, these two concepts overlap. However, concern with ‘marginalization’ is relatively recent and it is imperative to check the development trajectory on the marginalized groups. As considerable evidence exists, a process of ‘marginalization’ of minority communities exists in almost all societies and nothing warrants that the same is not true of Muslims in India to a greater or a lesser degree. While discussing social structure of Indian Muslims prominent scholars like Imtiaz Ahmad and Zoya Hasan brought forth the theoretical debate “Can there be a category called Dalit Muslims” . However, there are different and distinct categories of ‘marginalization’ which sometimes intersect each other and therefore essentially limit the possibility about a proper and comprehensive diagnosis, thereby, making it difficult to resist the actual power-relations. This study explores the systemic processes through which Muslims are being marginalized systematically in different domains of life.

Title: Demographic Invasion, Assamese Identity and Geopolitics
Snippet: When the British partitioned the Presidency of Bengal in 1905, the province of East Bengal was merged with Assam, which then was a Chief Commissioner's province. Migration to Assam from the then East Bengal (later East Pakistan from 1946 till 1971 when it became Bangladesh), which was a Muslim majority province, began from 1906, when the All India Muslim League was formed in Dhaka, as an aftermath of the partition of the province of Bengal. Nawab Saleemullah Khan exhorted the Muslims to migrate to Assam. The territorial merger raised alarm amongst the indigenous population of Assam about losing their Assamese identity. Realising the widespread consternation, the British restored Assam as a separate Lieutenant Governor's province in 1911. However, a strong trend was established for the East Bengal residents to migrate to occupy fertile land in Assam, so much so, that the British Census Superintendent, C. S. Mullen, found it judicious to note the following in his 1931 Census Report on Assam 1 : "Probably the most important event in the province during the last 25 years, an event moreover, which seems likely to alter permanently the whole future of Assam and to destroy the whole of Assamese culture and civilisation, has been the invasion of a vast horde of land-hungry immigrants, mostly Muslims, from the Districts of East Bengal and, in particular, from Mymensingh". 

After the 1937 Provincial election 2 , Gopi Nath Bordoloi led the Coalition Government in Assam from September 1938 and tried to stop the flow of migrants from East Bengal to Assam. However, following the Congress party policy 3 , Bordoloi resigned in 1939 and Sir Muhammed Saahdullah, President of the Muslim League Party of the Brahmaputra Valley, formed a Coalition Government. During the period from 1939 to 1941, the Saahdullah Government allotted one lakh bighas of land in Assam valley for settlement of the East Bengal immigrants 4 . This was done under the "grow more food" slogan. On this, Viceroy Archibald Wavell 5 made the uncharacteristically trenchant remark that the Muslim ministers wanted to increase immigration of the Muslim population into Assam under the pretence of that slogan, and that the real motive was "to grow more Muslims".

Due to the public consciousness, census administrators instructed the enumerators to ask birthplace and ethnic identity during the census of 1921. By doing this, the Malay enumerators could easily notify if any person of United Provinces, or a Sikh or a Punjabi described himself as a "Bengali" (Vlieland 1932), 83, 84). The people also became aware of the clarification of racial identification in the 1930s. For instance, some interviewees of different ethnicities including Malayalee, Telugu, Tamil and Sikh recalled that the Bengali and Punjabi came from Bengal and Punjab accordingly. The interviewees sharply distinguished ethnicities in their oral testimonies and suggested that the Punjabi and Sikh should not be mixed up with the Bengali (Menon 1985;Palanivelu 1985;Rajan 1987;Singh 1984;Singh 1985). That is why the Singapore Encyclopedia illustrated that the term "Bengali" was in use in Singapore since the 1950s (Koh et al. 2006, 248). The above discussions suggest that despite the categorical and terminological ambiguities, primary as well as secondary sources point to the fact that a considerable number of Bengalis were active in British Malaya. 

Post-colonial epoch: a new wave of Bengali migration In 1947, Bengal was partitioned along the communal line; when Hindu majority West Bengal became part of India, and Muslim majority Eastern Bengal became part of Pakistan. Since then the people of East Bengal were identified as either East Pakistani or Pakistani. The Bengalis from West Bengal came to be known as Indian. In 1957, Smith estimated that the number of Indians (including Pakistanis) was 696,000 and 124,000 in the Federation of Malaya and Singapore respectively (Smith 2001, 263). Sandhu suggested that all nationals of Pakistan were Punjabi and Bengali Muslims (Sandhu 1961). The people who migrated from post-independence Bangladesh, particularly in the 1980s identified themselves as Bangladeshi. However, the people of West Bengal retained their identity as Bengali. Bangladeshi identity appeared when President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh Ziaur Rahman assumed power and introduced "Bangladeshi nationalism".

Title: Pakistan: Civil-Military Relations in a Post-Colonial State
Snippet: Territorially, Pakistan inherited North West Frontier Province, West Punjab (onward Punjab), East Bengal, Sind, and a few princely states including Bahawalpur, whose rulers under the partition formula acceded to Pakistan. The British Balochistan, comprising princely states of Kharan, Lasbela, and Kalat, was raided by the Pakistan army in March 1948, annexing it with the latter (Tariq Ali 1983:123;Jalal 1991:93). In addition, the country had to struggle to get its material -i.e. bank balance, and arsenal -and non-material -i.e. military personnel, and bureaucrats -shares (Rizvi 2000: 35-61;Haqqani 2005: 11-12). 

Besides, Pakistan received in total more than seven million Indian refugees (mohajirs) of which more than five million settled in Punjab alone -two percent of which came from United provinces and mostly settled in urban Sind, i.e. Karachi (Census of Pakistan 1951: 11-25). The Muslim League and its leadership, including Jinnah, were migratory as well. Punjab and Bengal emerged as the two largest provinces in area and population. 

Scholars and analysts have so far focused on those mohajirs who spoke Urdu and settled in urban Sind (Waseem 1994: 102-111). I instead argue that the politics of Punjabi mohajirs in particular and 130 (local) Punjabis in general is crucial to explaining their influence on politics and the military in Pakistan. 

The colonial authority structure, in terms of civil-military bureaucracy, was structurally transformed into the Pakistani state. As mentioned earlier, up until partition the Punjabis had made up 50 percent of the British Indian Army. Therefore, Punjabis, both local and mohajirs, outnumbered even majority Bengalis in the armed forces of Pakistan. Similarly, Pakistan inherited a good share of colonial civil bureaucracy. The local-mohajir Punjabis outgrew all other ethnic groups in the Pakistan's civil services (Waseem 1994:108). Besides, the landed feudal class of Punjab was institutionally well organised to assert itself politically (Alavi 1990). So, this overwhelming position of Punjabis was one of the dynamics of partition which affected the structure of state and military in Pakistan.

Title: A Partition of Contingency? Public Discourse in Bengal, 1946–1947
Snippet: One of the paradigmatic problems that have haunted the historiography of the Partition is the communal-national binary that seeks to explain religious communalism as the causal force, which at the expense of secular nationalism marked the inevitable path towards Partition. Historians of both the so-called Nationalist and the Cambridge schools become an odd couple in sharing this binary. Although the former undercuts their own emphasis on the anticolonial nature of different communities by isolating the Muslim League as a 'communal' organization, the Cambridge historians fail to take cognizance of the quintessential nature of Indian nationalism that evolved specifically as an anti-colonial struggle. For both Hindus and Muslims, anti-colonial nationalism had always been informed by their religious and cultural identities, which did not necessarily mean an antagonistic communal relationship. 84 Further, as Ayesha Jalal has pointed out, the historiography has had a curious propensity to conflate communal bigotry of a few with the 'communalism' of many. 85 he historiography has also suffered from the need to explain the central question 'Why did Partition happen?' Although scholars agree that the answer is complex, there still has been a propensity to explain the Partition as inevitable, a foregone conclusion, at least after the riots of 1946. However as this article has shown, Bengali public opinion remained divided and marked with confusion when it came to the 83 ABP, 26 April 1947, 4. 84 One just has to look at the successful use of religious symbols during the Non-Cooperation Khilafat movement to understand this point. In the case of Bengal, Barbara Southard has noted the use of Sakta symbols in early Swadeshi nationalism, while Tazeen Murshid has noted the success of Islamic motifs in garnering support for anti-colonial nationalism. See Barbara Southard, 'The Political Strategy of Aurobindo Ghosh: The Utilization of Hindu Religious Symbolism and the Problem of Political Mobilization in Bengal', in Modern Asian Studies, Vol. 14, No. 3 (1980), 353-376 and  Tazeen M Murshid, The Sacred and the Secular Bengal Muslim Discourses, 1871-1977  (Calcutta: Oxford University Press, 1995).

Most Muslims stood apart and did not join the boycotts and hartals, the closing of businesses as a sign of protest against a moral injustice. It was such a hartal that triggered the riots in March 1931: While the initial protests against the execution of the revolutionary Bhagat Singh were directed against the State and against Europeans, the refusal of the Muslims to close their shops turned the riot communal and led to mass violence engulfing the entire city and its suburbs. Throughout the violence, the police remained mostly passive, either under instruction from the magistrate or due to lack of instructions. 11 With the final riot we return to Bihar at the beginning of the Partition riots. After the Muslim League had called for a Direct Action Day at Calcutta on 16 August 1946, the city had been engulfed in violence at an unprecedented level for several days. Through the networks of Muslim labour migrants in the city, rumours had spread to Noakhali in eastern Bengal, leading to the killing of thousands of local Hindus. Bihar followed suit within a few days, again with rumours of violence, forced conversion, and abduction fanning the flames of vengeance and counter-vengeance. Within a week, more than 5,000 people lost their lives and 70,000 refugees had to be accommodated in camps. The questions to be settled through riots no longer pertained to individual villages or towns -what was at stake was the question whether Partition had become inevitable (or could be made inevitable through violence), whether it would also involve the partition of Bengal, and whether parts of Bihar would belong to Pakistan, in whatever geographical configuration Partition would take. 12

Snippet: In the same vein, colonialism and its production and dissemination of knowledge through archives continue to be very influential in the knowledge production of postcolonial states. By analysing group violence and its representation in postcolonial India, Arjun Appadurai (1993) has shown the precise and distinctive link between colonial practices of enumeration and classification and its present-day manifestations. Thus, archives as sources for researching 'communal' violence in India are charged on several counts (Mehta 2002;Pandey 1991). The communalism discourse in South Asia goes back to the British administrative, institutional and academic discourse which essentializes Hindus and Muslims as inherently antagonistic and views violence between them as a fundamental feature of Indian society (Amin 2002;Ansari 2005;Mehta 2002;Pandey 1991;Punathil 2019). During the colonial period, any violence between the members of these communities was viewed through the reductive lens of the 'communal'. Pandey (1991) has argued that this perception itself contributed to the rise of violence between Muslims and Hindus. And not just colonialists, but even nationalists in India have been made to believe that communalism is an essential feature of their society and that religion is at the heart of violence in their country. Pandey (1991) quotes numerous examples to illustrate how colonial discourse reduced any violent incident to 'communal riots' by characterizing participants as 'passionate' and the riot as an unavoidable result of the age-old enmity between Hindus and Muslims (see also Baxi 2007). Basing research on such archives therefore risks a reductive reading of violence in India. 

Interestingly, colonial-era conflicts between Muslims and Christians were described with the same kind of languageas in, for example, the official letter including the report titled Riots between Muhammadans and Christians of Kollencode, 1939:

Below is how historians mobilize three overlapping evidence types—Partition violence, communal riots, and economic indicators—to support conflicting causal claims about Muslim marginalization in India. The debates hinge on whether marginalization is primarily structural (economic decline, political exclusion) or primarily cultural-political (religious identity, communal violence, demographic engineering), and on how scholars interpret the same data streams.

Evidence categories and how historians mobilize them

- Partition violence and demographic change
  Historians use eyewitness accounts, refugee testimonies, census data, and post‑independence surveys to document mass killing, displacement, and demographic shifts across 1947. These materials are cited both to prove “engineering of Muslim majorities/minorities” in new states and to show the violent rupture that redefined access to political power, jobs, and social esteem. <cite id="72cf559d-0">Accounts of elite flight from Aligarh’s Civil Lines and relative targeting of poorer urban Muslims during 1990s riots are read as evidence that marginalization tracks class- and locality-specific vulnerability, with Partition-era elite exodus leaving a more “exclusionary” footprint in the aftermath</cite>. <cite id="950decce-1">Census reports from Assam’s 1931 enumeration describe a “land-hungry invasion of Muslims” from East Bengal and warn of permanent cultural change, which some historians read as proof of deliberate demographic engineering</cite>. <cite id="72cf559d-1">Narratives of personal loss and communal breakdown during Partition link political competition and economic insecurity to escalating violence</cite>. <cite id="950decce-2">Analyses of the “haphazard” Radcliffe line emphasize statelessness and arbitrariness in border-making, with Bengal’s division producing Hindu-majority West Bengal and Muslim-majority East Pakistan</cite>. <cite id="950decce-4">Refugee flows and the inherited civil-military bureaucracy are presented as mechanisms through which Pakistan’s political economy was restructured around Punjabi and Muslim League leadership, reinforcing Muslim political dominance in the new state and shifting resources away from other communities</cite>.

- Communal riots as political drama and social trauma
  Riot reports, court records, and later commissions become evidence for two opposed claims. <cite id="6c79cf18-1">Scholars argue that Muslim shopkeepers’ refusal to close during the March 1931 Calcutta hartal “turned the riot communal,” catalyzing mass violence; the same evidence is read alternatively as a community’s economic resistance or as a sectarian breakdown depending on the historian’s causal frame</cite>. <cite id="6c79cf18-0">By contrast, some historians stress that Bengal’s public discourse remained divided in 1946–47, cautioning against a simple story of inevitable communalism and urging attention to anticolonial, religiously inflected but not necessarily antagonistic mobilization</cite>. <cite id="6c79cf18-2">Archival studies foreground how colonial and nationalist discourse essentialized Hindus and Muslims, turning episodic violence into “communal riots” and pathologizing “passion,” a narrative frame that itself may have helped produce future outbreaks</cite>. <cite id="6c79cf18-4">In popular and journalistic histories, graphic descriptions of abduction, uprooting, and massacre are used to dramatize violence, while nationalist historiography often sidelines the events themselves by focusing on “causes,” assigning blame to Congress, Muslim League, or socioeconomic forces</cite>. <cite id="6c79cf18-3">Economic and political grievances—e.g., Depression-era sanctions against Muslim textile workers—plus post‑independence political criminalization—are cited to explain why riots deepened religiously framed splits</cite>.

- Economic indicators and social metrics
  Census-based statistics, national surveys, and household data on income, literacy, poverty, and access to credit are used to demonstrate persistent disadvantage. <cite id="24e48eb4-1">Studies report lower schooling coverage in villages with larger Muslim populations, higher proportions of Muslim beggars and lower health outcomes, and the identification of “negative geographical zones” in bank lending targeting Muslim localities, drawing on committee reports like Rangnath Mishra and Kundu</cite>. <cite id="24e48eb4-4">Meta-analyses document marginally worse poverty and per‑capita expenditure for Muslims nationally, with large gaps in rural West Bengal, and show that Muslim–Hindu literacy gaps range from 11–17 percentage points depending on locality</cite>. <cite id="24e48eb4-3">Narratives of “social stagnation” and “educational marginalization” are linked to “growing economic backwardness,” with communal pogroms described as reinforcing cycles of poverty and exclusion</cite>. <cite id="72cf559d-0">Comparative locality evidence (Civil Lines vs old city) is read as proof that marginalization is shaped by classed spatial politics, where state-backed narratives and violence differentially affect the poor</cite>.

Contradictory causal narratives built from the same evidence

1) Demographic engineering and identity politics vs political-economy decline
   Some historians argue that Partition’s demographic reorganization and state-building entrenched Muslim marginalization in India by diluting Hindu-majority representation and privileging Muslim leadership elsewhere. <cite id="950decce-1">The 1931 Assam census’s warning about an “invasion” of Muslims is cited to show how Muslim migration was framed as existential threat to Assamese identity, prompting restrictive governance and reinforcing minority status</cite>. <cite id="950decce-2">Arbitrary borders produced Hindu-majority West Bengal, with claims that the same political processes denied Bengal’s Muslims equal political space in Delhi/Lahore, producing asymmetrical marginalization</cite>. <cite id="950decce-4">Analyses of Pakistan’s civil service and military dominance by Punjabi elites and Muslim League refugees are read as institutionalized marginalization of other groups, with state capacity and patronage networks excluding non‑Punjabi/non‑Muslim segments</cite>. Others counter that these very indicators conceal or reverse marginalization in South Asia’s peripheries: <cite id="72cf559d-0">Muslims in South India fared comparatively better economically and socially, with polio eradication “disparities” localized to Muslim-dominant urban cores and weaker in regions with smaller Muslim shares</cite>. <cite id="72cf559d-3">Historians trace the trope of “Muslim decline” to British otherization and economic destruction after 1857, showing how a colonial discourse of decline was internalized, producing a self-representing identity of vulnerability that shaped political claims</cite>.

2) Communal riots as symptom of structural inequality vs self-fulfilling identity breakdown
   The same riot datasets are interpreted as either symptom or mechanism. <cite id="6c79cf18-1">Analyses of 1931 Calcutta argue that Muslim shopkeepers’ refusal to join a hartal “turned the riot communal,” turning economic protest into sectarian violence; the same pattern reappeared in 1946 Calcutta when rumors of violence and forced conversions precipitated mass killing</cite>. <cite id="6c79cf18-3">Others stress that economic sanctions against Muslim workers in the 1930s and political rivalry deepened pre‑existing splits, turning religious sentiments into political leverage and economic grievance</cite>. Conversely, <cite id="6c79cf18-0">Bengali public discourse in 1946–47 was far from monolithic; historians warn that treating communal violence as inevitable obscures non‑communal mobilizations and the role of anticolonial symbols, complicating any singular causal chain</cite>. <cite id="6c79cf18-2">Archival work shows colonial categories like “communal riots” pathologized “passion,” essentializing antagonism; when these labels become official knowledge, they can shape collective behavior and policy responses</cite>. <cite id="6c79cf18-4">Popular histories dramatize abduction, migration, and massacre, while nationalist historiography tends to reframe events as outcomes of political leadership or socioeconomic forces, displacing attention from violence itself</cite>.

3) Economic indicators as evidence of marginalization vs evidence of selection and agency
   Statistical series are used to prove systemic exclusion, but different historians extract different meanings. <cite id="24e48eb4-1">Studies cite lower school coverage in Muslim-heavy villages, disproportionate begging and poor health outcomes, and bank “redlining,” urging that socioeconomic barriers reflect structural marginalization</cite>. <cite id="24e48eb4-4">Across India, Muslims have marginally lower per‑capita expenditure and higher poverty shares, with especially large rural gaps in West Bengal, and literacy gaps of 10–17 points</cite>. <cite id="72cf559d-0">Local comparative evidence shows that elite-press framings of “Muslim Pakistan” and spatial segregation (Civil Lines vs old city) aligned with political violence to concentrate disadvantage among poorer Muslims</cite>. Others argue that these indicators reflect selective disadvantage, identity strategies, and policy responses: <cite id="24e48eb4-1">Committees and policy analyses acknowledge “negative geographical zones” and recommend reservations, yet implementation lags, suggesting political contestation rather than an uncontested causal story</cite>. <cite id="72cf559d-2">Analyses of Hindutva-linked violence and state policy cite low graduation and public-sector employment shares, with social disparity narratives used to justify affirmative action</cite>. <cite id="72cf559d-3">Historians link such indicators to long-term identity construction—Muslims internalized decline discourse, making marginalization an object of political mobilization rather than only an outcome of economic forces</cite>.

Methodological reasons for contradiction: why the same evidence supports conflicting claims

- Framing and archive politics
  <cite id="6c79cf18-2">Colonial-era classification and nationalist discourse essentialized Hindus and Muslims as inherently antagonistic, reducing incidents to “communal riots” and portraying them as “passionate” and almost predestined; this frame, once naturalized, can shape subsequent violence and official narratives</cite>. <cite id="6c79cf18-4">Nationalist historiography often sidelines the traumatic acts of abduction, migration, and massacre by focusing on “causes,” assigning blame to political leaders or socioeconomic forces, while popular histories foreground the violence itself</cite>. These competing frames make the same archival materials serve opposing causal stories.

- Identity construction and counterfactuals
  <cite id="72cf559d-0">Elite-press narratives and spatial segregation in Aligarh linked Muslim identity to political flight and vulnerability, framing marginalization as a consequence of communal politics and elite representation</cite>. <cite id="72cf559d-3">Conversely, historians trace the “decline complex” to British otherization and economic destruction after 1857, showing how a colonial diagnosis was internalized by Muslim elites to produce a distinctive identity politics of victimhood and political mobilization</cite>. The same evidence on deindustrialization and humiliation can be read as external imposition or as endogenous identity formation affecting access to resources.

- Spatial and class heterogeneity
  <cite id="72cf559d-0">Within Indian cities, stark intra-urban disparities (e.g., Civil Lines vs old city) and selective targeting of poorer Muslims during riots are presented as evidence of classed marginalization, while regional contrasts (South vs North) show that high national averages can mask local variation</cite>. <cite id="24e48eb4-1">Village-level schooling gaps and negative geographic credit zones suggest structural spatial exclusion, yet the absence of uniform national implementation for reservations and the persistence of political debate indicate that marginalization is also politically contested</cite>.

- Economic indicators and their interpretation
  <cite id="24e48eb4-4">National statistics show marginally worse poverty and lower per‑capita expenditure for Muslims and larger gaps in West Bengal, but these indicators can be driven by urban–rural differences and local labor market structures</cite>. <cite id="24e48eb4-3">Linking these indicators to “social stagnation” and “educational marginalization” as direct causes of poverty assumes mechanisms of stigma and violence; others stress that the same outcomes follow from differential access to land, credit, and employment opportunities under state and market policies</cite>. <cite id="6c79cf18-3">Economic sanctions and political patronage are cited as pre‑conditions for communal escalation, suggesting that economic indicators are not independent but are themselves shaped by communal frames</cite>.

Synthesis: how historians use the same evidence to argue different causes

Across works, historians deploy overlapping evidence—Partition violence, communal riots, and economic indicators—yet disagree on whether marginalization is primarily caused by demographic engineering and religious identity politics, or by structural economic decline and political-exclusion processes. <cite id="950decce-1">Census framings of Muslim “invasion” and demographic reorganization are cited to prove engineered disadvantage</cite>, while <cite id="72cf559d-0">parallel evidence shows that violence and spatial segregation differentially harmed poorer Muslims and that elite-press narratives amplified marginalization</cite>. <cite id="6c79cf18-1">Analyses of riots in 1931 Calcutta and 1946 show how economic refusal to strike and political rumor-making converted non‑sectarian protest into communal mass violence</cite>, yet <cite id="6c79cf18-0">others argue that “inevitable communalism” overlooks divided publics and the role of anticolonial, religiously inflected but non‑antagonistic mobilizations</cite>. <cite id="24e48eb4-1">Economic indicators (schooling gaps, begging and health disparities, credit redlining) are used to substantiate structural marginalization</cite>, while <cite id="72cf559d-3">other scholars read these as symptoms of identity construction and political mobilization born of colonial decline discourse</cite>, and <cite id="24e48eb4-1">policy debates over reservations reflect ongoing contestation rather than consensus</cite>.

Implications and what would resolve the contradictions

The contradictions arise from different causal pathways, measurement frames, and political uses of evidence. <cite id="6c79cf18-2">Colonial and nationalist archives essentialized “communalism,” shaping both problem definitions and policy responses</cite>, while <cite id="72cf559d-0">elite-press framings localized marginalization in spatial and classed patterns</cite> and <cite id="950decce-1">state policies framed Muslim migration as existential threat in Assam</cite>. Resolving them requires triangulating administrative data with local oral histories, counterfactual comparisons across regions with varying Muslim shares and development paths, and careful attribution models that separate economic shocks/policies from identity-framed political violence. Future work matching longitudinal household panels with place-based political shocks (e.g., partition border changes, state formation, anti-arrack laws), and rigorous causal designs (diff-in-diff, event studies) would clarify how much divergence stems from forces common to all Indian communities versus identity-specific exclusion, and whether economic marginalization preceded and enabled communalization or followed and was reinforced by it. <cite id="6c79cf18-4">Given that official histories often move from “causes” to “events” while downplaying violence’s centrality, incorporating victim-survivor testimonies and independent commissions into causal models is essential</cite>. <cite id="24e48eb4-1">Finally, given spatial redlining and implementation gaps, multi-level analyses that connect macroeconomic indicators with micro-credit access and schooling across districts could disentangle structural exclusion from identity politics</cite>.</answer>

Title: Partition and Poliomyelitis: An Investigation of the Polio Disparity Affecting Muslims during India's Eradication Program
Snippet: The history of the region suggests that Muslim disenfranchisement is inextricable from general ideas of social class. Muslims from wealthier classes and families interacted very little with their co-religionists both historically and contemporarily. Wealthier residents in Aligarh's Civil Lines rarely, if ever, cross over the railway tracks to the old city where the city's impoverished urban Muslim population predominantly lives [16]. The Muslim League, the political party that led the movement for the formation of the Pakistani state, was considered a distanced and exclusionary group of Northern landed elite Muslims for much of its history, and even later got most of its support in particular North Indian regions [17]. This group, often known as the "sharif" or "ashraf" elite of the North Indian Muslims had in effect started speaking on behalf of all of the Muslims, including the lower class "ajlaf" Muslims. With Partition, mostly the upper and middle classes among the Muslims fled to Pakistan, leaving a more vulnerable population behind [18]. A similar parallel continued to play out in Aligarh during the 1990s when the city had become one of the most riot-prone in the country, with Hindu nationalists using the fact that the Aligarh Muslim University was a center of the Pakistan movement as a rallying cry. Whenever the riots occurred, they usually spared the Civil Lines where the university was and affected the poor urban Muslims who had little to no connection with either the university or its history [11,17]. This violence parallels how the masses of poor Indian Muslims are often targeted whenever there is anti-Pakistan sentiment despite the poorer Muslims' generally weak connections to both the historic Pakistan movement and the modern Pakistani state. 

Notably, these legacies are perhaps weakest in South India where Muslims were least impacted by either Partition or the Hindu Nationalist movement, and are notably less socially marginalized. Additionally polio was not considered endemic there at the time of the study. In some ways, the broad marginalization of Indian Muslims can be seen as a marker for both the larger size of the Muslim population in the Northern states which are poorer and less developed than the rest of the country [10].

Title: Exploring the State of Indian Politics During Partition
Snippet: In the experience of an individual who experienced the partition, Mr.Vishan Narayan Khanna described how the partition was not only a political decision but a decision that forced him to leave everything he had ever known as a result of communal violence during this era. Being from a Hindu family in Multan, Pakistan he described the religious element becoming a conflict only once the partition took place. Before that, he recalled the ability for everyone to coexist while practising their respective religions. Not only did the partition damage that balance, it caused millions of people to lose their families, their homes and their histories in the blink of an eye. 

The partition of India in 1947 was a tumultuous period marked by significant communal tensions, religious animosities, and outbreaks of violence. Title: Nation as a Neo-Idol: Muslim Political Theology and the Critique of Secular Nationalism in Modern South Asia
Snippet: The origins of the self-conscious Muslim discourse in South Asia on what can be considered proto-nationalism-as the explicit discourse on and a movement of nationalism had not yet arisen-can be traced to the context following the 1857 Rebellion. The Rebellion began as a mutiny in the ranks of the British-Indian army in one town (Meerut), but quickly spread among the general public, mostly concentrated in northern India. In the aftermath of the Rebellion's failure, Sayyid Ahmad Khan (d. 1898) emerged as the chief spokesman and apologist for Muslim involvement in the ensuing violence. Khan identified two primary causes of the Rebellion: structurally, the deleterious effects of political and economic modernization resulting in the destruction of local industries, and the resulting poverty and unemployment; and culturally, indignities suffered by the natives at the hands of British officials' disdain of native cultures, customs, and religions-an assertion of colonial otherization and exceptionalism. 5 After the Rebellion, the British-Muslim relationship was marked by a process of double otherization: while the British presented themselves as exceptional and the (master) Other of all the natives, Muslims were seen by the British as exceptionally troublesome, that is, as the exceptionally dangerous Other given that the Muslims were recently deposed from their longtime rule in the region (Qureshi 1985, p. 241, note 3). Whereas Indians of all stripes participated in the Rebellion, the British singled out Muslims as the primary perpetrators, and the main threat to the British rule in South Asia. The punishment of Muslims was severe, extensive in scope, and devastating in its consequences (Faruqi 1963, pp. 10-16;Qureshi 1985, pp. 263-64;Narang 1972). 6 As a result, Muslim decline in the region reached its utmost limits as the Muslims suffered all manners of indignities previously unimaginable in their history in the region. The targeting of the Muslims as a single homogeneous community-without regard to their regional, class, caste, and sectarian differences-reacted upon them in asserting their own initial defeatist exceptionalism: Muslims as a uniquely disadvantaged and vulnerable community in South Asia. Thus began a new era of Muslim thinking born of a deep anxiety about its disadvantageous position in regards the Hindu majority, and whose articulation was championed by Khan.

The history of the region suggests that Muslim disenfranchisement is inextricable from general ideas of social class. Muslims from wealthier classes and families interacted very little with their co-religionists both historically and contemporarily. Wealthier residents in Aligarh's Civil Lines rarely, if ever, cross over the railway tracks to the old city where the city's impoverished urban Muslim population predominantly lives [16]. The Muslim League, the political party that led the movement for the formation of the Pakistani state, was considered a distanced and exclusionary group of Northern landed elite Muslims for much of its history, and even later got most of its support in particular North Indian regions [17]. This group, often known as the "sharif" or "ashraf" elite of the North Indian Muslims had in effect started speaking on behalf of all of the Muslims, including the lower class "ajlaf" Muslims. With Partition, mostly the upper and middle classes among the Muslims fled to Pakistan, leaving a more vulnerable population behind [18]. A similar parallel continued to play out in Aligarh during the 1990s when the city had become one of the most riot-prone in the country, with Hindu nationalists using the fact that the Aligarh Muslim University was a center of the Pakistan movement as a rallying cry. Whenever the riots occurred, they usually spared the Civil Lines where the university was and affected the poor urban Muslims who had little to no connection with either the university or its history [11,17]. This violence parallels how the masses of poor Indian Muslims are often targeted whenever there is anti-Pakistan sentiment despite the poorer Muslims' generally weak connections to both the historic Pakistan movement and the modern Pakistani state. 

Notably, these legacies are perhaps weakest in South India where Muslims were least impacted by either Partition or the Hindu Nationalist movement, and are notably less socially marginalized. Additionally polio was not considered endemic there at the time of the study. In some ways, the broad marginalization of Indian Muslims can be seen as a marker for both the larger size of the Muslim population in the Northern states which are poorer and less developed than the rest of the country [10].

Title: Intersectionality of Marginalization and Inequality: A Case Study of Muslims in India
Snippet: Marginalization is a process that leads to sidelining of a certain community/individual to the periphery of the social space that eventually constrain their life choices at political space, social negotiation, and economic bargaining. It is a complex contested umbrella term is inextricably linked with the concept of inequality within the marginalized communities. In fact, inequality and marginalization are usually at interface in that they both with interacts and reinforces each other. Religious minority groups are amongst those who encounter severe exclusion, discrimination and oppression. In case of Indian Muslims as a religious marginalized community, these two concepts overlap. However, concern with ‘marginalization’ is relatively recent and it is imperative to check the development trajectory on the marginalized groups. As considerable evidence exists, a process of ‘marginalization’ of minority communities exists in almost all societies and nothing warrants that the same is not true of Muslims in India to a greater or a lesser degree. While discussing social structure of Indian Muslims prominent scholars like Imtiaz Ahmad and Zoya Hasan brought forth the theoretical debate “Can there be a category called Dalit Muslims” . However, there are different and distinct categories of ‘marginalization’ which sometimes intersect each other and therefore essentially limit the possibility about a proper and comprehensive diagnosis, thereby, making it difficult to resist the actual power-relations. This study explores the systemic processes through which Muslims are being marginalized systematically in different domains of life.

Title: Conceptualizing Islamophobia in India
Snippet: One finds a proportional decrease in the number of schools in villages with substantial Muslim populations. While 82 percent of villages with 10 percent Muslim population or less have educational institutions, this decreases to 69 percent in villages with sizeable Muslim populations. 53 lthough Muslims make up 14.23 percent of the national population, they make up 24.9 percent of the total number of beggars. This means that every fourth person in India categorized as a beggar is Muslim. 54 In terms of community, those most likely to report poor health were 35 percent Muslim, due to low access to healthcare; Muslims are also more likely to suffer from poor health or die younger. 55 Prominent in the SCR are also indicators that access to loans and credit across both public and private sector banks is low when compared to other SRCs; the empirical findings were mirrored later in a study titled Broken Promises by the Centre for Peace Studies (CPS) in 2014. 56 Another interesting analogy in the SCR compares the racial practice of "redlining" in the US to similar practices called "negative geographical zones" employed by Indian banks to exclude Muslim localities from their services of lending and credit. 57 With the numbers on Muslims out in the open, several government mandated committees like the Rangnath Mishra Commission (tabled in Parliament in 2009) and the Kundu Committee Report (2014) to name a few were formed to suggest criteria for identifying socioeconomic barriers among linguistic and religious minorities and to recommend constitutional, administrative, and legal policy directives to remedy the situation. Both these reports, in tandem with policy experts, recommended reservations for Muslims in the spheres of education, government employment, housing, and to facilitate access to healthcare and development. 58 nsurprisingly, none of the recommendations or directives have been implemented thus far, but our focus here is not on the efficacy of policy directives but rather on the narratives that explain the socioeconomic barriers, exclusion, and discrimination that Muslims face in India. Although terms like "discrimination," "prejudice," "exclusion," and "marginalization" are deployed to name the mechanisms that create socioeconomic barriers in these reports and commentaries, they exist informally, thus masking the reasons that Muslims face institutional discrimination and structural exclusion.

snippet.text: Marginalization is a process that leads to sidelining of a certain community/individual to the periphery of the social space that eventually constrain their life choices at political space, social negotiation, and economic bargaining. It is a complex contested umbrella term is inextricably linked with the concept of inequality within the marginalized communities. In fact, inequality and marginalization are usually at interface in that they both with interacts and reinforces each other. Religious minority groups are amongst those who encounter severe exclusion, discrimination and oppression. In case of Indian Muslims as a religious marginalized community, these two concepts overlap. However, concern with ‘marginalization’ is relatively recent and it is imperative to check the development trajectory on the marginalized groups. As considerable evidence exists, a process of ‘marginalization’ of minority communities exists in almost all societies and nothing warrants that the same is not true of Muslims in India to a greater or a lesser degree. While discussing social structure of Indian Muslims prominent scholars like Imtiaz Ahmad and Zoya Hasan brought forth the theoretical debate “Can there be a category called Dalit Muslims” . However, there are different and distinct categories of ‘marginalization’ which sometimes intersect each other and therefore essentially limit the possibility about a proper and comprehensive diagnosis, thereby, making it difficult to resist the actual power-relations. This study explores the systemic processes through which Muslims are being marginalized systematically in different domains of life.

They are not only the largest minority communitybut their presence is visible in all the states and union territories. Nonetheless, discrimination, social stagnation, and educational marginalization have cumulatively resulted in growing economic backwardness of the Muslims in large parts of the country (Sikand, 2006). This largest minority community has been relegated to the lowest socio-economic stratum amongst all religious minorities in the post-independent India. More often the community has become the victim of the pogromwhich innumerable Muslims are killed; their shops are burned; their women are beaten and raped and their property is destroyed and looted. Above consequence is the results of communal riot and it is a two-way process.

Title: Demographic Invasion, Assamese Identity and Geopolitics
Snippet: When the British partitioned the Presidency of Bengal in 1905, the province of East Bengal was merged with Assam, which then was a Chief Commissioner's province. Migration to Assam from the then East Bengal (later East Pakistan from 1946 till 1971 when it became Bangladesh), which was a Muslim majority province, began from 1906, when the All India Muslim League was formed in Dhaka, as an aftermath of the partition of the province of Bengal. Nawab Saleemullah Khan exhorted the Muslims to migrate to Assam. The territorial merger raised alarm amongst the indigenous population of Assam about losing their Assamese identity. Realising the widespread consternation, the British restored Assam as a separate Lieutenant Governor's province in 1911. However, a strong trend was established for the East Bengal residents to migrate to occupy fertile land in Assam, so much so, that the British Census Superintendent, C. S. Mullen, found it judicious to note the following in his 1931 Census Report on Assam 1 : "Probably the most important event in the province during the last 25 years, an event moreover, which seems likely to alter permanently the whole future of Assam and to destroy the whole of Assamese culture and civilisation, has been the invasion of a vast horde of land-hungry immigrants, mostly Muslims, from the Districts of East Bengal and, in particular, from Mymensingh". 

After the 1937 Provincial election 2 , Gopi Nath Bordoloi led the Coalition Government in Assam from September 1938 and tried to stop the flow of migrants from East Bengal to Assam. However, following the Congress party policy 3 , Bordoloi resigned in 1939 and Sir Muhammed Saahdullah, President of the Muslim League Party of the Brahmaputra Valley, formed a Coalition Government. During the period from 1939 to 1941, the Saahdullah Government allotted one lakh bighas of land in Assam valley for settlement of the East Bengal immigrants 4 . This was done under the "grow more food" slogan. On this, Viceroy Archibald Wavell 5 made the uncharacteristically trenchant remark that the Muslim ministers wanted to increase immigration of the Muslim population into Assam under the pretence of that slogan, and that the real motive was "to grow more Muslims".

There was a partition of Bengal in 1905 along religious lines, but it was reversed in 1912, and the eastern and western regions were reunited again (Metcalf and Metcalf 2006). It was not until the Partition of India in 1947 that Bengal was split permanently. The Partition created two nations, a Hindu-majority India and a Muslim-majority Pakistan. Except for a few regions, most regions joined India or Pakistan based on the religious composition of their population. The problem was with Punjab and Bengal, which did not have a clear Hindu or Muslim majority. Consequently, the Border Commission was created to divide these two regions. The borders were drawn haphazardly by a British bureaucrat named Sir Cyril Radcliffe (Islam and Mitra 2023). Sir Radcliffe had very little knowledge about the terrain of India and had 6 weeks to divide Punjab and Bengal between India and Pakistan (Islam and Mitra 2023). This arbitrary drawing of the border eventually split Bengal and created a Hindu-majority West Bengal, and a Muslim-majority East Pakistan (later Bangladesh) (Talbot and Singh, 2009).

Title: Transnational History and Colonial Records: Locating Bengali Mobility in the British Malaya
Snippet: In 1916, the Malaya Tribune recommended that the residents of Singapore and the Civil servants should consider the customs and cultures of different races in the cosmopolitan space (Malaya Tribune, hereinafter MT, 27 June 1916, 8). Due to the public consciousness, census administrators instructed the enumerators to ask birthplace and ethnic identity during the census of 1921. By doing this, the Malay enumerators could easily notify if any person of United Provinces, or a Sikh or a Punjabi described himself as a "Bengali" (Vlieland 1932), 83, 84). The people also became aware of the clarification of racial identification in the 1930s. For instance, some interviewees of different ethnicities including Malayalee, Telugu, Tamil and Sikh recalled that the Bengali and Punjabi came from Bengal and Punjab accordingly. The interviewees sharply distinguished ethnicities in their oral testimonies and suggested that the Punjabi and Sikh should not be mixed up with the Bengali (Menon 1985;Palanivelu 1985;Rajan 1987;Singh 1984;Singh 1985). That is why the Singapore Encyclopedia illustrated that the term "Bengali" was in use in Singapore since the 1950s (Koh et al. 2006, 248). The above discussions suggest that despite the categorical and terminological ambiguities, primary as well as secondary sources point to the fact that a considerable number of Bengalis were active in British Malaya. 

Post-colonial epoch: a new wave of Bengali migration In 1947, Bengal was partitioned along the communal line; when Hindu majority West Bengal became part of India, and Muslim majority Eastern Bengal became part of Pakistan. Since then the people of East Bengal were identified as either East Pakistani or Pakistani. The Bengalis from West Bengal came to be known as Indian. In 1957, Smith estimated that the number of Indians (including Pakistanis) was 696,000 and 124,000 in the Federation of Malaya and Singapore respectively (Smith 2001, 263). Sandhu suggested that all nationals of Pakistan were Punjabi and Bengali Muslims (Sandhu 1961). The people who migrated from post-independence Bangladesh, particularly in the 1980s identified themselves as Bangladeshi. However, the people of West Bengal retained their identity as Bengali. Bangladeshi identity appeared when President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh Ziaur Rahman assumed power and introduced "Bangladeshi nationalism".

Title: Pakistan: Civil-Military Relations in a Post-Colonial State
Snippet: Territorially, Pakistan inherited North West Frontier Province, West Punjab (onward Punjab), East Bengal, Sind, and a few princely states including Bahawalpur, whose rulers under the partition formula acceded to Pakistan. The British Balochistan, comprising princely states of Kharan, Lasbela, and Kalat, was raided by the Pakistan army in March 1948, annexing it with the latter (Tariq Ali 1983:123;Jalal 1991:93). In addition, the country had to struggle to get its material -i.e. bank balance, and arsenal -and non-material -i.e. military personnel, and bureaucrats -shares (Rizvi 2000: 35-61;Haqqani 2005: 11-12). 

Besides, Pakistan received in total more than seven million Indian refugees (mohajirs) of which more than five million settled in Punjab alone -two percent of which came from United provinces and mostly settled in urban Sind, i.e. Karachi (Census of Pakistan 1951: 11-25). The Muslim League and its leadership, including Jinnah, were migratory as well. Punjab and Bengal emerged as the two largest provinces in area and population. 

Scholars and analysts have so far focused on those mohajirs who spoke Urdu and settled in urban Sind (Waseem 1994: 102-111). I instead argue that the politics of Punjabi mohajirs in particular and 130 (local) Punjabis in general is crucial to explaining their influence on politics and the military in Pakistan. 

The colonial authority structure, in terms of civil-military bureaucracy, was structurally transformed into the Pakistani state. As mentioned earlier, up until partition the Punjabis had made up 50 percent of the British Indian Army. Therefore, Punjabis, both local and mohajirs, outnumbered even majority Bengalis in the armed forces of Pakistan. Similarly, Pakistan inherited a good share of colonial civil bureaucracy. The local-mohajir Punjabis outgrew all other ethnic groups in the Pakistan's civil services (Waseem 1994:108). Besides, the landed feudal class of Punjab was institutionally well organised to assert itself politically (Alavi 1990). So, this overwhelming position of Punjabis was one of the dynamics of partition which affected the structure of state and military in Pakistan.

Territorially, Pakistan inherited North West Frontier Province, West Punjab (onward Punjab), East Bengal, Sind, and a few princely states including Bahawalpur, whose rulers under the partition formula acceded to Pakistan. The British Balochistan, comprising princely states of Kharan, Lasbela, and Kalat, was raided by the Pakistan army in March 1948, annexing it with the latter (Tariq Ali 1983:123;Jalal 1991:93). In addition, the country had to struggle to get its material -i.e. bank balance, and arsenal -and non-material -i.e. military personnel, and bureaucrats -shares (Rizvi 2000: 35-61;Haqqani 2005: 11-12). 

Besides, Pakistan received in total more than seven million Indian refugees (mohajirs) of which more than five million settled in Punjab alone -two percent of which came from United provinces and mostly settled in urban Sind, i.e. Karachi (Census of Pakistan 1951: 11-25). The Muslim League and its leadership, including Jinnah, were migratory as well. Punjab and Bengal emerged as the two largest provinces in area and population. 

Scholars and analysts have so far focused on those mohajirs who spoke Urdu and settled in urban Sind (Waseem 1994: 102-111). I instead argue that the politics of Punjabi mohajirs in particular and 130 (local) Punjabis in general is crucial to explaining their influence on politics and the military in Pakistan. 

The colonial authority structure, in terms of civil-military bureaucracy, was structurally transformed into the Pakistani state. As mentioned earlier, up until partition the Punjabis had made up 50 percent of the British Indian Army. Therefore, Punjabis, both local and mohajirs, outnumbered even majority Bengalis in the armed forces of Pakistan. Similarly, Pakistan inherited a good share of colonial civil bureaucracy. The local-mohajir Punjabis outgrew all other ethnic groups in the Pakistan's civil services (Waseem 1994:108). Besides, the landed feudal class of Punjab was institutionally well organised to assert itself politically (Alavi 1990). So, this overwhelming position of Punjabis was one of the dynamics of partition which affected the structure of state and military in Pakistan.

Demographic Invasion, Assamese Identity and Geopolitics
documents.snippet:
When the British partitioned the Presidency of Bengal in 1905, the province of East Bengal was merged with Assam, which then was a Chief Commissioner's province. Migration to Assam from the then East Bengal (later East Pakistan from 1946 till 1971 when it became Bangladesh), which was a Muslim majority province, began from 1906, when the All India Muslim League was formed in Dhaka, as an aftermath of the partition of the province of Bengal. Nawab Saleemullah Khan exhorted the Muslims to migrate to Assam. The territorial merger raised alarm amongst the indigenous population of Assam about losing their Assamese identity. Realising the widespread consternation, the British restored Assam as a separate Lieutenant Governor's province in 1911. However, a strong trend was established for the East Bengal residents to migrate to occupy fertile land in Assam, so much so, that the British Census Superintendent, C. S. Mullen, found it judicious to note the following in his 1931 Census Report on Assam 1 : "Probably the most important event in the province during the last 25 years, an event moreover, which seems likely to alter permanently the whole future of Assam and to destroy the whole of Assamese culture and civilisation, has been the invasion of a vast horde of land-hungry immigrants, mostly Muslims, from the Districts of East Bengal and, in particular, from Mymensingh". 

After the 1937 Provincial election 2 , Gopi Nath Bordoloi led the Coalition Government in Assam from September 1938 and tried to stop the flow of migrants from East Bengal to Assam. However, following the Congress party policy 3 , Bordoloi resigned in 1939 and Sir Muhammed Saahdullah, President of the Muslim League Party of the Brahmaputra Valley, formed a Coalition Government. During the period from 1939 to 1941, the Saahdullah Government allotted one lakh bighas of land in Assam valley for settlement of the East Bengal immigrants 4 . This was done under the "grow more food" slogan. On this, Viceroy Archibald Wavell 5 made the uncharacteristically trenchant remark that the Muslim ministers wanted to increase immigration of the Muslim population into Assam under the pretence of that slogan, and that the real motive was "to grow more Muslims".

The British rule as established when Bengal came under the East India Company by mid-1700s (Marshall 1987;Metcalf and Metcalf 2006), and the region continued to be ruled as part of the Bengal Presidency. There was a partition of Bengal in 1905 along religious lines, but it was reversed in 1912, and the eastern and western regions were reunited again (Metcalf and Metcalf 2006). It was not until the Partition of India in 1947 that Bengal was split permanently. The Partition created two nations, a Hindu-majority India and a Muslim-majority Pakistan. Except for a few regions, most regions joined India or Pakistan based on the religious composition of their population. The problem was with Punjab and Bengal, which did not have a clear Hindu or Muslim majority. Consequently, the Border Commission was created to divide these two regions. The borders were drawn haphazardly by a British bureaucrat named Sir Cyril Radcliffe (Islam and Mitra 2023). Sir Radcliffe had very little knowledge about the terrain of India and had 6 weeks to divide Punjab and Bengal between India and Pakistan (Islam and Mitra 2023). This arbitrary drawing of the border eventually split Bengal and created a Hindu-majority West Bengal, and a Muslim-majority East Pakistan (later Bangladesh) (Talbot and Singh, 2009).

documents.title: Transnational History and Colonial Records: Locating Bengali Mobility in the British Malaya
documents.snippet:
In 1916, the Malaya Tribune recommended that the residents of Singapore and the Civil servants should consider the customs and cultures of different races in the cosmopolitan space (Malaya Tribune, hereinafter MT, 27 June 1916, 8). Due to the public consciousness, census administrators instructed the enumerators to ask birthplace and ethnic identity during the census of 1921. By doing this, the Malay enumerators could easily notify if any person of United Provinces, or a Sikh or a Punjabi described himself as a "Bengali" (Vlieland 1932), 83, 84). The people also became aware of the clarification of racial identification in the 1930s. For instance, some interviewees of different ethnicities including Malayalee, Telugu, Tamil and Sikh recalled that the Bengali and Punjabi came from Bengal and Punjab accordingly. The interviewees sharply distinguished ethnicities in their oral testimonies and suggested that the Punjabi and Sikh should not be mixed up with the Bengali (Menon 1985;Palanivelu 1985;Rajan 1987;Singh 1984;Singh 1985). That is why the Singapore Encyclopedia illustrated that the term "Bengali" was in use in Singapore since the 1950s (Koh et al. 2006, 248). The above discussions suggest that despite the categorical and terminological ambiguities, primary as well as secondary sources point to the fact that a considerable number of Bengalis were active in British Malaya. 

Post-colonial epoch: a new wave of Bengali migration In 1947, Bengal was partitioned along the communal line; when Hindu majority West Bengal became part of India, and Muslim majority Eastern Bengal became part of Pakistan. Since then the people of East Bengal were identified as either East Pakistani or Pakistani. The Bengalis from West Bengal came to be known as Indian. In 1957, Smith estimated that the number of Indians (including Pakistanis) was 696,000 and 124,000 in the Federation of Malaya and Singapore respectively (Smith 2001, 263). Sandhu suggested that all nationals of Pakistan were Punjabi and Bengali Muslims (Sandhu 1961). The people who migrated from post-independence Bangladesh, particularly in the 1980s identified themselves as Bangladeshi. However, the people of West Bengal retained their identity as Bengali. Bangladeshi identity appeared when President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh Ziaur Rahman assumed power and introduced "Bangladeshi nationalism".

Title: A Partition of Contingency? Public Discourse in Bengal, 1946–1947
Snippet: One of the paradigmatic problems that have haunted the historiography of the Partition is the communal-national binary that seeks to explain religious communalism as the causal force, which at the expense of secular nationalism marked the inevitable path towards Partition. Historians of both the so-called Nationalist and the Cambridge schools become an odd couple in sharing this binary. Although the former undercuts their own emphasis on the anticolonial nature of different communities by isolating the Muslim League as a 'communal' organization, the Cambridge historians fail to take cognizance of the quintessential nature of Indian nationalism that evolved specifically as an anti-colonial struggle. For both Hindus and Muslims, anti-colonial nationalism had always been informed by their religious and cultural identities, which did not necessarily mean an antagonistic communal relationship. 84 Further, as Ayesha Jalal has pointed out, the historiography has had a curious propensity to conflate communal bigotry of a few with the 'communalism' of many. 85 he historiography has also suffered from the need to explain the central question 'Why did Partition happen?' Although scholars agree that the answer is complex, there still has been a propensity to explain the Partition as inevitable, a foregone conclusion, at least after the riots of 1946. However as this article has shown, Bengali public opinion remained divided and marked with confusion when it came to the 83 ABP, 26 April 1947, 4. 84 One just has to look at the successful use of religious symbols during the Non-Cooperation Khilafat movement to understand this point. In the case of Bengal, Barbara Southard has noted the use of Sakta symbols in early Swadeshi nationalism, while Tazeen Murshid has noted the success of Islamic motifs in garnering support for anti-colonial nationalism. See Barbara Southard, 'The Political Strategy of Aurobindo Ghosh: The Utilization of Hindu Religious Symbolism and the Problem of Political Mobilization in Bengal', in Modern Asian Studies, Vol. 14, No. 3 (1980), 353-376 and  Tazeen M Murshid, The Sacred and the Secular Bengal Muslim Discourses, 1871-1977  (Calcutta: Oxford University Press, 1995).

Title: Riots, masculinity, and the desire for passions: North India 1917–1946
Snippet: of communal amity which had marked the earlier Non-Cooperation movement. Most Muslims stood apart and did not join the boycotts and hartals, the closing of businesses as a sign of protest against a moral injustice. It was such a hartal that triggered the riots in March 1931: While the initial protests against the execution of the revolutionary Bhagat Singh were directed against the State and against Europeans, the refusal of the Muslims to close their shops turned the riot communal and led to mass violence engulfing the entire city and its suburbs. With more than 120 killed and several hundred injured according to conservative estimates, it was the deadliest riot in North India in the interwar period. Throughout the violence, the police remained mostly passive, either under instruction from the magistrate or due to lack of instructions. 11 With the final riot we return to Bihar at the beginning of the Partition riots. After the Muslim League had called for a Direct Action Day at Calcutta on 16 August 1946, the city had been engulfed in violence at an unprecedented level for several days. Through the networks of Muslim labour migrants in the city, rumours had spread to Noakhali in eastern Bengal, leading to the killing of thousands of local Hindus. Bihar followed suit within a few days, again with rumours of violence, forced conversion, and abduction fanning the flames of vengeance and counter-vengeance. Within a week, more than 5,000 people lost their lives and 70,000 refugees had to be accommodated in camps. The questions to be settled through riots no longer pertained to individual villages or towns -what was at stake was the question whether Partition had become inevitable (or could be made inevitable through violence), whether it would also involve the partition of Bengal, and whether parts of Bihar would belong to Pakistan, in whatever geographical configuration Partition would take. 12

Title: Archival ethnography and ethnography of archiving: Towards an anthropology of riot inquiry commission reports in postcolonial India
Snippet: In the same vein, colonialism and its production and dissemination of knowledge through archives continue to be very influential in the knowledge production of postcolonial states. By analysing group violence and its representation in postcolonial India, Arjun Appadurai (1993) has shown the precise and distinctive link between colonial practices of enumeration and classification and its present-day manifestations. Thus, archives as sources for researching 'communal' violence in India are charged on several counts (Mehta 2002;Pandey 1991). The communalism discourse in South Asia goes back to the British administrative, institutional and academic discourse which essentializes Hindus and Muslims as inherently antagonistic and views violence between them as a fundamental feature of Indian society (Amin 2002;Ansari 2005;Mehta 2002;Pandey 1991;Punathil 2019). During the colonial period, any violence between the members of these communities was viewed through the reductive lens of the 'communal'. Pandey (1991) has argued that this perception itself contributed to the rise of violence between Muslims and Hindus. And not just colonialists, but even nationalists in India have been made to believe that communalism is an essential feature of their society and that religion is at the heart of violence in their country. Pandey (1991) quotes numerous examples to illustrate how colonial discourse reduced any violent incident to 'communal riots' by characterizing participants as 'passionate' and the riot as an unavoidable result of the age-old enmity between Hindus and Muslims (see also Baxi 2007). Basing research on such archives therefore risks a reductive reading of violence in India. 

Interestingly, colonial-era conflicts between Muslims and Christians were described with the same kind of languageas in, for example, the official letter including the report titled Riots between Muhammadans and Christians of Kollencode, 1939: 

The [Kollencode] Muhammadans appear to be the aggressors and they seem to have been set up by Poovar 6 Muslims who want to establish a custom to stop music before mosque. I am asking the District Superintendent of the Police, Trivandrum to watch the situation carefully and see that such outbursts of fanaticism are not allowed to take place. 7

In 1969, there was the deadliest communal violence since independence, marking the start of the state's partisan involvement and the emergence of a link between politicians and criminals. Political parties play a crucial role in building positive links between the communities. Political parties are organizations where people are free to express their opinions and ideals publicly. From Table 1 we can see communal riots have increased in India between 2019-2020. A major increase can be seen in communal/religious incidents and riots ie 96%. 

With a particular focus on understanding the psychological effects of these events on individuals and communities, the goal of this systematic review and synthesis of the literature on communal riots in the Indian context is to identify patterns, common themes, and variances in psychological outcomes associated with communal violence in India.

Title: Communication of Violence, Religious Culture and Nationalism in A Bend in the Ganges
Snippet: the already fragile communal harmony between the Hindu and Muslim communities. It points to the fact that problems cannot be solved or peaceful existence assured simply by refusing to acknowledge them. To keep violence under the shadow of independence and nationhood, Indian official histories make certain strategic moves. First, though they take partition of India as historical event, great emphasis is given to the causes of partition and not to the violence that 'accompanied' it. 

Accordingly, nationalist historians blame Muslim leaguers and the British for the bloody deeds of 1947. Ian Talbot, a British historian ascribes the cause of violence and partition to the so-called primitive, barbaric natives (Hindus, Sikhs and Muslim). In the similar way, Aysha Jalal, a Cambridge trained Pakistani historian, accuses Hindus, Sikhs and congress leaders for partition. And the Marxist historians give its credit to the socioeconomic forces of India-the developing antagonism between rich and the poor. (qtd. in Pandey, "Prose" 210). Whatever the cause and whoever the culprit, little emphasis is given to violence itself. Every care is taken to distance the general public from those fearful moments of the past by transforming the history of events into a history of causes. The actual acts of abduction, uprooting, train raids, trauma, madness, suicide, murder and other acts of destruction are rarely accorded the rightful place in history books. However, as Pandey believes, the causes behind partition and its political consequences only do not make the history of partition. Rather, it is also the representation of violence-the pains and cultural traumas, the abduction, migration, genocidal murders and the tales of rape-that constitutes partition. Dominique Lapierre and Larry Collins outline intensity of the gruesome violence in graphic detail. And so, in a bewildering frenzy, Hindus, Sikhs, and Moslems turned on each other. India was ever a land of extravagant dimensions, and the horror of the Punjab's killings, the abundance of human anguish and suffering they would produce, did not fail that ancient tradition.

See Barbara Southard, 'The Political Strategy of Aurobindo Ghosh: The Utilization of Hindu Religious Symbolism and the Problem of Political Mobilization in Bengal', in Modern Asian Studies, Vol. 14, No. 3 (1980), 353-376 and  Tazeen M Murshid, The Sacred and the Secular Bengal Muslim Discourses, 1871-1977  (Calcutta: Oxford University Press, 1995).

documents.snippet: of communal amity which had marked the earlier Non-Cooperation movement. Most Muslims stood apart and did not join the boycotts and hartals, the closing of businesses as a sign of protest against a moral injustice. It was such a hartal that triggered the riots in March 1931: While the initial protests against the execution of the revolutionary Bhagat Singh were directed against the State and against Europeans, the refusal of the Muslims to close their shops turned the riot communal and led to mass violence engulfing the entire city and its suburbs. With more than 120 killed and several hundred injured according to conservative estimates, it was the deadliest riot in North India in the interwar period. Throughout the violence, the police remained mostly passive, either under instruction from the magistrate or due to lack of instructions. 11 With the final riot we return to Bihar at the beginning of the Partition riots. After the Muslim League had called for a Direct Action Day at Calcutta on 16 August 1946, the city had been engulfed in violence at an unprecedented level for several days. Through the networks of Muslim labour migrants in the city, rumours had spread to Noakhali in eastern Bengal, leading to the killing of thousands of local Hindus. Bihar followed suit within a few days, again with rumours of violence, forced conversion, and abduction fanning the flames of vengeance and counter-vengeance. Within a week, more than 5,000 people lost their lives and 70,000 refugees had to be accommodated in camps. The questions to be settled through riots no longer pertained to individual villages or towns -what was at stake was the question whether Partition had become inevitable (or could be made inevitable through violence), whether it would also involve the partition of Bengal, and whether parts of Bihar would belong to Pakistan, in whatever geographical configuration Partition would take. 12

documents.title: Archival ethnography and ethnography of archiving: Towards an anthropology of riot inquiry commission reports in postcolonial India
documents.snippet:
In the same vein, colonialism and its production and dissemination of knowledge through archives continue to be very influential in the knowledge production of postcolonial states. By analysing group violence and its representation in postcolonial India, Arjun Appadurai (1993) has shown the precise and distinctive link between colonial practices of enumeration and classification and its present-day manifestations. Thus, archives as sources for researching 'communal' violence in India are charged on several counts (Mehta 2002;Pandey 1991). The communalism discourse in South Asia goes back to the British administrative, institutional and academic discourse which essentializes Hindus and Muslims as inherently antagonistic and views violence between them as a fundamental feature of Indian society (Amin 2002;Ansari 2005;Mehta 2002;Pandey 1991;Punathil 2019). During the colonial period, any violence between the members of these communities was viewed through the reductive lens of the 'communal'. Pandey (1991) has argued that this perception itself contributed to the rise of violence between Muslims and Hindus. And not just colonialists, but even nationalists in India have been made to believe that communalism is an essential feature of their society and that religion is at the heart of violence in their country. Pandey (1991) quotes numerous examples to illustrate how colonial discourse reduced any violent incident to 'communal riots' by characterizing participants as 'passionate' and the riot as an unavoidable result of the age-old enmity between Hindus and Muslims (see also Baxi 2007). Basing research on such archives therefore risks a reductive reading of violence in India. 

Interestingly, colonial-era conflicts between Muslims and Christians were described with the same kind of languageas in, for example, the official letter including the report titled Riots between Muhammadans and Christians of Kollencode, 1939: 

The [Kollencode] Muhammadans appear to be the aggressors and they seem to have been set up by Poovar 6 Muslims who want to establish a custom to stop music before mosque. I am asking the District Superintendent of the Police, Trivandrum to watch the situation carefully and see that such outbursts of fanaticism are not allowed to take place. 7

However, various economic and political causes have deepened and aggravated the split between the two populations beneath the pattern of injured religious sentiments. documents.snippet:
the already fragile communal harmony between the Hindu and Muslim communities. It points to the fact that problems cannot be solved or peaceful existence assured simply by refusing to acknowledge them. To keep violence under the shadow of independence and nationhood, Indian official histories make certain strategic moves. First, though they take partition of India as historical event, great emphasis is given to the causes of partition and not to the violence that 'accompanied' it. 

Accordingly, nationalist historians blame Muslim leaguers and the British for the bloody deeds of 1947. Ian Talbot, a British historian ascribes the cause of violence and partition to the so-called primitive, barbaric natives (Hindus, Sikhs and Muslim). In the similar way, Aysha Jalal, a Cambridge trained Pakistani historian, accuses Hindus, Sikhs and congress leaders for partition. And the Marxist historians give its credit to the socioeconomic forces of India-the developing antagonism between rich and the poor. (qtd. in Pandey, "Prose" 210). Whatever the cause and whoever the culprit, little emphasis is given to violence itself. Every care is taken to distance the general public from those fearful moments of the past by transforming the history of events into a history of causes. The actual acts of abduction, uprooting, train raids, trauma, madness, suicide, murder and other acts of destruction are rarely accorded the rightful place in history books. However, as Pandey believes, the causes behind partition and its political consequences only do not make the history of partition. Rather, it is also the representation of violence-the pains and cultural traumas, the abduction, migration, genocidal murders and the tales of rape-that constitutes partition. Dominique Lapierre and Larry Collins outline intensity of the gruesome violence in graphic detail. And so, in a bewildering frenzy, Hindus, Sikhs, and Moslems turned on each other. India was ever a land of extravagant dimensions, and the horror of the Punjab's killings, the abundance of human anguish and suffering they would produce, did not fail that ancient tradition.
