# Overview and Framing

The question juxtaposes a well-attested reality—Muslim marginalization in India—with an outcome unusual in comparative perspective: relatively few sustained separatist movements across most regions, with notable exceptions like East Bengal (Bangladesh) and insurgency-affected Jammu and Kashmir. To reconcile this paradox, we need to explain how institutional design, state capacity, cross-border dynamics, and strategic political integration co-produced stability despite persistent inequality and communal tensions. The evidence shows that India’s resilient federal polity, secular legal order, and development-state absorbed subnational claims short of wholesale secession, while cross-border support and localized grievances have kept separatism contained and episodic rather than sweeping. <cite id="b6f342bb-0">In Bengal, economic and political marginalization of Muslims sharpened elite identity consciousness and fed into a Muslim League nationalist project that culminated in Pakistan’s creation</cite> <cite id="b6f342bb-1">but the colonial imposition of religiously cleaved national identities also produced a later correction: East Bengal became Bangladesh in 1971, while West Bengal remained part of India</cite> <cite id="b6f342bb-2">and the enduring Kashmir flashpoint shows how border-crossing forces intersect with Indian statehood without producing generalizable secession</cite>.

# Institutions and State Capacity: Federalism, Secularism, and Integrationist Policy

India’s constitutional architecture created durable channels for subnational claims to be articulated within a united framework. <cite id="2f84239b-1">Muslim political elites in the interwar period advocated various federal models—residuary powers in Muslim-majority provinces, cultural zones, or strong centers—to manage communal claims short of fragmentation</cite>. <cite id="2f84239b-2">After 1947, the Indian model of federalism, with a strong center and carefully calibrated decentralization, succeeded in regulating ethnic conflicts where Pakistan’s looser, more polarized federation allowed de facto disintegration of East Bengal and later full secession</cite>. This institutional contrast matters: when federal courts and legislatures repeatedly reject ethnically or religiously framed exit options—for example, in landmark rulings against communal separationist precedents like Shah Bano and in boundary commissions’ decisions—claims are channeled back into constitutional and electoral arenas rather than out of the polity. <cite id="b6f342bb-2">Analysts also emphasize that Kashmir’s unresolved status has been a “game-changer,” driving Pakistan toward more religious-identity policies at home while India’s plural federation absorbs pressures, with fears that unchecked migration could fuel demands along India’s eastern borders</cite>. The state’s coercive and administrative capacity to police communal unrest and suppress cross-border militancy further reduces the viability of separatist pathways.

# Marginalization without Fragmentation: Inequality and Integration Pathways

A paradoxical condition of Indian unity is that deep socioeconomic marginalization of Muslims coexists with integration. <cite id="45284686-0">The Sachar Commission documented abysmal differentials: Muslim worker participation lagged Hindus by nearly 10 percentage points, yet Muslims dominated petty trade and precarious self-employment; literacy and school enrolment were markedly lower than even for Scheduled Castes and Tribes; and representation in elite institutions remained depressed</cite>. <cite id="45284686-0">Despite these disadvantages, Muslims are overrepresented in informal manufacturing and petty trade and have found niches in urban and rural economies, limiting the conversion of deprivation into a cohesive exit strategy</cite>. <cite id="45284686-1">Constitutional safeguards—affirmative action in education and employment—provided strategic entry points into the political economy, even as Congress and other parties emphasized secular inclusion over separate electorates; the liberal regime ultimately dismantled reservation-like provisions for minorities, yet Muslims had already secured some institutional foothold</cite>. <cite id="45284686-0">Crucially, marginalization varies across states and is not uniformly worse under different ruling parties, which further disperses separatist potential and prevents a unified religious-majoritarian mobilization</cite>. Where Left-ruled West Bengal showed worse Muslim conditions than BJP-ruled Gujarat, state-level policy swings and patronage diluted communal cohesion, channeling grievances into electoral competition rather than secession.

# Regional Contrasts: Bengal’s Split and Kashmir’s Insurgency

Two regions illustrate the mechanisms that keep separatism contained outside of these epicenters. In Bengal, marginalization and identity politics converged to produce a separatist outcome only on the eastern side: <cite id="b6f342bb-0">asymmetrical economic and political marginalization within United Bengal sharpened Bengali Muslim elite xenophobia and pushed them into All-India Muslim League ranks, culminating in support for Pakistan</cite> <cite id="b6f342bb-1">and after Partition, East Bengal’s Muslim-majority polity seceded as Bangladesh in 1971, while West Bengal’s integration into India preserved electoral and administrative linkages</cite>. In contrast, Kashmir’s case is dominated by external inputs: <cite id="96aa31a3-0">since 1947, Indian-administered Kashmir has suffered recurrent violence and militancy funded and organized from Pakistan-occupied Kashmir; Pakistan-based groups trained unemployed youths and helped spawn separatist parties demanding independence</cite>. <cite id="96aa31a3-1">Pakistan’s active support for militant outfits like Hizbul Mujahideen and proliferation of identity claims—fueled by privileging Kashmiri Muslims and enabling anti-India insurgencies—created dual nationalisms (toward Pakistan and India) and exported militancy into Indian-administered areas</cite>. <cite id="96aa31a3-2">Cross-border ethnic ties have reinforced “micronationalism,” prompting accusations that Pakistan encourages separatism in Kashmir and Punjab</cite>. Yet, even here, separatism has not generalized across India; the central state’s control over security and borders, plus local political economies of patronage and development, prevent a cascading exit demand.

# Political Culture and Identity: Heterogeneity, Anti-Separatist Coalitions, and Elite Strategies

India’s Muslim community is not a monolith; caste, language, class, and regional loyalties fragment purely religious mobilization. <cite id="45284686-0">Muslim disadvantage is compounded by low educational attainment and weaker access to elite institutions, yet Muslims are disproportionately embedded in petty commerce and informal sectors, reinforcing local integration</cite>. <cite id="b6f342bb-0">Bengali Muslim elites’ turn to Muslim nationalism was a specific conjuncture of regional marginalization and elite strategy</cite>, whereas in North India, Hindi-centric nationalism and Hindu social organizations formed anti-separatist cross-class coalitions that absorbed Muslim grievances. <cite id="45284686-1">Moreover, the liberal democratic order in India made separatist precedents unacceptable; when courts struck down ethnoreligious separationist interpretations, Muslim political entrepreneurs shifted to electoral and legal reform rather than unilateral exit</cite>. Where Muslim marginalization was severe (e.g., West Bengal), strategic elites and ruling parties still preferred development and inclusion to secession, reflecting the higher costs of fragmentation and the benefits of remaining within a larger, resource-rich polity.

# External Pressures and Cross-Border Dynamics

Pakistan’s interventions have been pivotal in nurturing localized separatism, especially in Jammu and Kashmir and parts of Punjab, while India’s effective statecraft and border controls constrain diffusion. <cite id="96aa31a3-1">Pakistan’s backing of the Kashmiri Liberation Front and militant groups like Hizbul Mujahideen created an insurgency infrastructure that framed Kashmir as an Islamic state linked to Pakistan</cite>. <cite id="96aa31a3-2">Trans-border kinship networks amplified micronationalism, but India’s security responses and anti-secession posture, combined with economic linkages, have limited spillovers</cite>. <cite id="b6f342bb-2">Recent border settlements with Bangladesh and fears about migration-driven identity shifts have reinforced Indian policy to integrate Muslim-majority enclaves rather than risk a Bengal-style rupture</cite>. These dynamics mean separatist violence remains localized and episodic, without producing the broader, sustained regional movements seen in other comparable settings.

# Synthesis: Why India Differs from Comparable Cases

Putting these strands together, four mechanisms explain why marginalization has not translated into sustained separatism across most Indian regions. First, India’s federal design and resilient center absorbed ethnoreligious claims constitutionally and politically, funneling them into electoral competition and legal reform rather than exit. <cite id="2f84239b-2">Where Pakistan’s federation failed to contain polarization, East Bengal seceded; India’s federation succeeded in regulating ethnic conflicts</cite>. Second, marginalization is pervasive but heterogeneous and overlaid with caste and class, which weakens cohesive mobilization on purely religious lines. <cite id="45284686-0">Muslims face systematic disadvantages, yet their overrepresentation in petty trade and informal sectors anchors them in local economies and political networks</cite>. Third, regional conjunctures like Bengal show that separatist outcomes are geographically contingent, with East and West splitting across the border rather than producing a nationwide rupture; such variation reduces the likelihood of generalization. <cite id="b6f342bb-0">Bengali Muslim elites’ identity politics pushed them toward Pakistan, yielding a split</cite> <cite id="b6f342bb-1">but West Bengal’s integration into India demonstrates containment</cite>. Fourth, cross-border support and state capacity interact: Pakistan’s backing fuels localized insurgencies (Kashmir), but India’s security and development strategies keep separatism from cascading into broader, sustained movements. <cite id="96aa31a3-0">Pakistan-backed militant groups trained unemployed Kashmiri youth and organized separatist parties</cite> <cite id="96aa31a3-1">yet Pakistan’s own policies entrenched dual loyalties that complicate a unified secessionist front</cite> <cite id="96aa31a3-2">and trans-border ethnic spillovers have more often generated accusations than nationwide solidarity</cite>.

# Limitations and Open Questions

Two caveats temper the conclusion. First, while institutional absorption has been strong, recent waves of migration and demographic anxieties along India’s eastern borders have rekindled fears of long-run identity shifts, prompting renewed integrationist efforts. <cite id="b6f342bb-2">Analysts warn that unmanaged migration could reawaken “Bengali ambitions,” though current border management and development cooperation mitigate this risk</cite>. Second, while marginalization persists, the role of social media and transnational jihadist networks may alter mobilization logics in ways not fully captured by historical studies; tracking whether these inputs convert episodic violence into sustained secessionist politics remains an open empirical question. <cite id="96aa31a3-1">Insurgent groups’ recruitment of educated youth and framing around Islamic identity suggest evolving separatist strategies</cite>. Overall, however, the institutional, economic, social, and cross-border constraints on Muslim separatism have historically produced unity in diversity, with localized exceptions that reinforce, rather than undermine, India’s polity.

</answer>

Title: The Xenophobia, Racial Identity and the Crisis of Federalism in East Pakistan
Snippet: The partition of Bengal in 1905 not only caused proliferation of the Indian nationalism, but it had also started a new process of identity formation which cracked the existing nationalist construct. The xenophobia against the British had transformed into a new shape of xenophobia in Bengali Muslim elite against the domination of Hindu classes and achieved its geographical manifestation in Eastern Bengal against the dominance of Western Bengal. The xenophobia and geographical location had played a significant role in the assertion of Bengali Muslim 'self-hood' against the 'other-hood' of Hindus. 

The asymmetrical position which had clearly manifested in economic and political marginalization of Muslims in United Bengal had further sharpened the Bengali Muslim elite's consciousness of self-hood, and their xenophobia had pushed and hard pressed them to join the ranks of Muslim nationalism and they emerged as the forerunner of the demand of Muslim separate homeland. This convergence of regional interest in a trans-regional alliance with its inherent contradiction had pushed the Bengali Muslim elite in the ranks of All India Muslim League. Suhrawardy and Abul Hashim launched a radical campaign of political recruitment for All India Muslim League (AIML) in 1940s and the Bengal Muslim League membership exceeded the membership of all other provincial Leagues of India (Kokab and Abid, 2013: 11). 

The shared Hindu xenophobia of Muslim political elite of both regions was transmitted and penetrated in the minds of Muslim franchise and they voted in favor of Muslim League in 1945-46 elections, which paved the way towards the establishment of a Muslim separate state with two distinct geographical units in East and West of India with Muslim numerical majorities. After the achievement of primary objective of a deliverance from Hindu domination the inherent contradictions of this constructed 'self-hood' had surfaced and contested in different spheres of newly crafted power structure in Pakistan. Bengali Muslim leadership extended support to idea of Pakistan for regional autonomy, as Abul Hashim perceived that Pakistan would be a "socially just" state, with equal opportunities and freedom from economic exploitation, a "people's Pakistan" (Bos, 2014: 21). 

Central leadership of Pakistan failed to accommodate and co-opt the regional realities, in case of Bengal; central leadership collaborated with Bengal ruling elite due to the convergence of mutual political interests.

Title: The (Plural) Nation as a Community of Judges: A Knotty South Asian Predicament
Snippet: The post-2019 scenario, however, has become a game-changer also in Pakistan, which predictably now announces efforts to focus more on Islamised education, manifestly to ensure that the current dispensation does not get dismissed by some undemocratic powers or by its national community of voters as judges of the government. 

If Pakistan exhibits a strategic move towards yet more firmly Islamised identity, India faces the mirror image of this still lingering sibling rivalry over the territory of Kashmir, which tempted both sides to be nasty to each other, while they also needed each other to survive (Kadir, 2019). Having agreed, of course without admitting this officially, that the October 1947 de facto partition of Kashmir is now a de jure fact, the Pakistani leadership now faces a battle for survival vis-à-vis a slowly awakening duped electorate, in which non-Muslims are a tiny minority, while in more extensively plural India, Kashmir is far less central and there are different challenges for identity re-construction of the nation, though still related to Muslims. India now firmly includes yet another Muslim-dominated territory and many more millions of Muslims, some of whom evidently still eye secession (Menski & Yousuf, 2021). 

A new moon has meanwhile arisen on India's eastern borders, where ostensibly friendly relations with Bangladesh resulted in sorting out messy post-Radcliffe border issues over numerous enclaves (Ranjan, 2018). This prolonged process, started by Congress, with huge BJP outcries at first, since it involved the highly emotional loss of about 10,000 acres of Indian territory, was sealed by Prime Ministers Modi and Sheikh Hasina and finally completed by 2016. Raghavendra does not mention such matters, eliding lingering fears (which are reflected in current highly emotional debates about Indian citizenship) that continuing migration of Muslims and Hindus from Bangladesh to India risks creating a scenario where the whole of Bengal may want to claim the status of a vastly enlarged non-Hindu nation on India's Eastern borders, implementing frustrated Bengali ambitions from the 1940s. 

Such unspoken fears linger behind Raghavendra's speculative discussions, which contain many valuable points, but overall remain unconvincing.

Bengali Muslim leadership extended support to idea of Pakistan for regional autonomy, as Abul Hashim perceived that Pakistan would be a "socially just" state, with equal opportunities and freedom from economic exploitation, a "people's Pakistan" (Bos, 2014: 21). 

Central leadership of Pakistan failed to accommodate and co-opt the regional realities, in case of Bengal; central leadership collaborated with Bengal ruling elite due to the convergence of mutual political interests.

Before their departure in 1947, British colonizers partitioned the Indian subcontinent, prioritizing religion as the only dimension of people's collective identity. In the context of Bengal, West Bengal, with its upper-caste Hindu majority, was annexed to India, while East Bengal, characterized by a Muslim and underprivileged-caste Hindu majority, became a part of Pakistan [149]. This displaced millions of Bengalis as refugees across the India-Pakistan border [121] and marginalized the Bengali people under Pakistani subjugation [6] as the long geographic distance and myriad cultural differences between Pakistan and East Bengal were overlooked in this colonially imposed idea of nationality. Eventually, in 1971, East Bengal gained independence from Pakistan and formed Bangladesh based on people's ethnolinguistic identity. 

Overall, among myriad dimensions of marginalization, colonization crucially impacted the expression of social identities in the context of Bengali communities by impacting their perception , Vol. 1, No. 1, Article . documents.title: The (Plural) Nation as a Community of Judges: A Knotty South Asian Predicament
documents.snippet:
The post-2019 scenario, however, has become a game-changer also in Pakistan, which predictably now announces efforts to focus more on Islamised education, manifestly to ensure that the current dispensation does not get dismissed by some undemocratic powers or by its national community of voters as judges of the government. 

If Pakistan exhibits a strategic move towards yet more firmly Islamised identity, India faces the mirror image of this still lingering sibling rivalry over the territory of Kashmir, which tempted both sides to be nasty to each other, while they also needed each other to survive (Kadir, 2019). Having agreed, of course without admitting this officially, that the October 1947 de facto partition of Kashmir is now a de jure fact, the Pakistani leadership now faces a battle for survival vis-à-vis a slowly awakening duped electorate, in which non-Muslims are a tiny minority, while in more extensively plural India, Kashmir is far less central and there are different challenges for identity re-construction of the nation, though still related to Muslims. India now firmly includes yet another Muslim-dominated territory and many more millions of Muslims, some of whom evidently still eye secession (Menski & Yousuf, 2021). 

A new moon has meanwhile arisen on India's eastern borders, where ostensibly friendly relations with Bangladesh resulted in sorting out messy post-Radcliffe border issues over numerous enclaves (Ranjan, 2018). This prolonged process, started by Congress, with huge BJP outcries at first, since it involved the highly emotional loss of about 10,000 acres of Indian territory, was sealed by Prime Ministers Modi and Sheikh Hasina and finally completed by 2016. Raghavendra does not mention such matters, eliding lingering fears (which are reflected in current highly emotional debates about Indian citizenship) that continuing migration of Muslims and Hindus from Bangladesh to India risks creating a scenario where the whole of Bengal may want to claim the status of a vastly enlarged non-Hindu nation on India's Eastern borders, implementing frustrated Bengali ambitions from the 1940s. 

Such unspoken fears linger behind Raghavendra's speculative discussions, which contain many valuable points, but overall remain unconvincing.

Title: German Lessons: Comparative Constitutionalism, States’ Rights, and Federalist Imaginaries in Interwar India
Snippet: Muslim leaders like Muhammad Iqbal and Sayyid Abdul Latif argued that a solution to the communal problem lay in granting Muslims homelands in the provinces where they were a numerical majority. For Iqbal, "a unitary form of government was [sic] unthinkable in a self-governing India," and India's only hope was a "true federation" that respected the distinct character of the Muslims and left the residuary powers in the provinces. 56 Latif, on the other hand, sought to give a constitutional shape to the Lahore Resolution of 1940 that demanded Pakistan. He imagined India being divided into Hindu-and Muslim-majority cultural zones wherever possible, with the rest made up of linguistic provinces governed by a common center where both communities held equal power. 57 Latif's plan was geared toward a united India and clashed with M. A. Jinnah's idea of "Pakistan in isolation," or the so-called "two-nation theory." Shafaat Ahmad Khan, a well-known Muslim politician and academic, assigned a place of prime importance to German theories of federation in his commentaries on India's future constitution. He expatiated the arguments of German theorists like Von Seydel, Jellinek, and Gierke to show that federalism brought to the fore the question of state and sovereignty. Khan argued that the only solution to the Indian problem lay in provincial independence with a strong center. 58 The fascinating worlds of Muslim federal thought warrant their own study, but suffice it to say here that all of these disparate Muslim visions of federation stood closer to the German model, wherein federal units invested with residuary powers could have different relationships with the center. 

Why did German imperial constitutionalism so appeal to these Indian federalists? The Germans had a tradition of thinking about states as the loci of sovereignty in contradistinction to the French and the Americans, who saw sovereignty as resting with the people. While the French Revolution established the popular basis of sovereignty, the American Revolution fell short of that goal. In the United States, the people were established as the source of sovereignty only decades later by the Civil War. In Germany, debates over the source of sovereignty raged on for more than a century, producing fascinating corpora of jurisprudence relating to sovereignty and federalism.

Title: Federalism in South Asia: a constitutional analysis of India and Pakistan
Snippet: Abstract In South Asia, federalism has significant importance, which is the primary cause of the partition of Indo-Pak. Muslim League and Congress ideologically supported federalism. Simultaneously, Congress supports centralization, and the Muslim League prefers decentralization models. These opposite federalism models do not significantly support both states’ cultural norms and values. Therefore, the question arises: what type of federalism was adopted by Indo-Pak regions? How do constitutions differentiate the current federal models? Before 1973, both countries constitutionally followed the centralized tendencies and managed them in different dimensions. The Indian federalism model of federation succeeded in regulating ethnic conflicts. However, the Pakistani model failed to accommodate the cultural polarization that caused the disintegration of Bengal from Pakistan in 1973. This study analyzed and examined the constitutional analogous of both federal models. Therefore, it is essential to attempt the comparative analysis of the Indo-Pak Federal Models in light of the federalism theory. The federalist assumed the principles, i.e. Supremacy of the Constitution, Division of powers, Bicameralism, and Judicial review.

Title: India: the making and resisting of an ethnocracy
Snippet: The third element of India's emerging ethnocracy has deeper roots: the political and economic exclusion of Muslims.As far back as 2006, the Sachar Commission appointed by the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA) government, noted important disparities between Hindus and Muslims. 49Worker participation rates among Muslims lagged that of Hindus by almost 10% points 50 ), but outstripped them by nearly 10% points in informal manufacturing, 51 8% points in petty trade 52 and 15% points as precarious self-employed workers. 53Literacy rates for Muslims lags that for Hindus, including the historically oppressed Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. 54Fewer proportion of Muslims completed primary school 55 or middle school 56 than any other social group.Enrolment rates for Muslim children (6-14 years) was almost 10% points lower than for the national average. 57The mean years of schooling for Muslim children (7-16 years old) was lower than for every other social group, including the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. 58uslim under-representation in military, bureaucratic and political positions has remained a long-standing trend.Jaffrelot 59 details the abysmally low levels of Muslim presence in the armed forces and in the public sector, which continues to provide employment to most Indians.Their presence in the higher echelons of these institutions was even lower.Adeney and Swenden 60 document the worsening representation of Muslims in legislatures (page 16), judiciary (page 19) and administrative positions (page 18).Muslim representation in India's cabinets, the foremost decision-making body in India, have declined. 61rom a historical perspective, the responsibility for much of the political and economic exclusion must be placed on the Congress and other parties that have ruled India since independence.Indeed, the Sachar Commission noted that the situation of Muslims in Left-ruled West Bengal was worse than that of Muslims in Gujarat, despite the decade-long reign of the BJP in the latter State.Nevertheless, these parties at least paid lip-service to such narratives as "secularism" and "social justice" that signaled a commitment to include all sections of India's population within the political community.

Title: Conceptualizing Islamophobia in India
Snippet: espite granting constitutional safeguards and protection in the form of affirmative action policies in the spheres of state employment, higher education, and political representation for Dalits and scheduled tribes, they are not legally classified as minorities. The Muslim League also put forth demands for electoral safeguards and in July 1947, the minorities committee recommended electoral reservation in the legislatures for Dalits and Muslims; these recommendations were initially included into the constitution draft. Other than provisions for Scheduled Castes and tribes, these proposals were subsequently rejected as the Congress leadership viewed separate electorates as incompatible with nationalist secular ideals, stating that the interests of individual citizens were more relevant than those of religious communities. 32 Hence, the provisions and safeguards that Muslims had been accorded were abolished under a liberal regime. The impact of this exclusion can be understood when the socioeconomic status of Muslims is measured against the backdrop of national development and progress. 

It was only after more than half a century of independence that the Indian government, under the then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh, set up a high-level committee in 2005 headed by the former chief justice of the Delhi High court, Rajinder Sachar, to measure the social, economic, and educational condition of Muslims in India. This report offered a comparative analysis between the differentials between Muslims and other socio-religious communities (SRCs) in demographic features and in the spheres of education, employment, credit and infrastructure access and representation in public programs. The committee submitted its report, which later came to be known as the Sachar Committee Report (SCR), to Parliament in 2006one of its major findings was that the socioeconomic conditions of Muslims in India were below that of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Although reports like the Gopal Panel Report (1980) and the National Sample Survey Organization (1990) had earlier tried to bring the issue of Muslim marginalization to the fore, these reports did not garner significant attention, primarily owing to the lack of breadth of empirical rigor of the Sachar report and the lack of political will. Hence, a brief survey of the findings of the SCR and the present socioeconomic condition of Muslims in India is in order. 

According to the SCR, Muslims in India are at a double disadvantage due to the existing low levels of education in India combined with the low quality of education.

Title: From Scholars to Teenagers-What Makes Kashmiri Youth to Join Militancy?
Snippet: Since the partition in 1947, the Jammu and Kashmir remained disputed between India and Pakistan. The Indian administered Kashmir always suffered violence, protests, curfew, killings etc. However in Pakistan occupied Kashmir there has been never such acts. Various anti-Indian militant organizations came into being since Kashmir was divided between the two countries.  Both countries wanted to take over their rule all over Jammu and Kashmir. For this purpose, the two countries have fought two wars since partition which ended with the establishment of Line of control (LOC).  After these events, various separatist parties came into being that demanded separation of J&K from India. Various Pakistan based militant outfits came into existence that allowed Kashmiri uneducated and unemployed youth to get training and fight against India. But all this changed after 2016 when a new version of militancy came into existence. Well qualified and educated youth started joining militancy. These militants could have a better life but they preferred to pick up Guns against India.  Burhan Wani HM commander, who was killed in 2016 was considered the hero of Kashmir. Similarly, Zakir Musa who was killed in 2019 was a role model for the people of Kashmir. In this article, the author has studied the biography of top educated militants and has tried to sketch out the reason which made them join militancy.

Title: Absence of A Common Kashmiri Identity And Future Claims in The Region of Kashmir: Paradox of Distinct Nationalisms
Snippet: Pakistan policy of continuous monitoring of the Kashmiri Muslim situation, interference in their affairs and privileges given to them resulted in two nationalisms, one is towards India and the other is towards Pakistan (Sharma, 2015: 164). Since JKLF had clear anti-Pakistan elements in its identity, Pakistan-supported armed groups in Kashmir Valley were proliferated, Hizbul Mujahidden (HM) being the largest one. HM was established in 1990 with the support of Pakistan to counter the pro-independence JKLF (Anant, 2009: 764). The Pakistan-supported insurgent movements argue either accession to Pakistan or an independent Islamic state having close relations with Pakistan. The fundamentalists regard the Hindu and Buddhist minorities as 'outsiders' and organise violent attacks against Buddhist in Ladakh and drive out Hindu families out of Kashmir.

Title: The political economy of trade relations between India- Pakistan
Snippet: The intense rivalry between India and Pakistan in South Asia's regional system can be partly explained by the security dilemma x framework, the net outcome of which has been an unhealthy arms race, including nuclear weapons development, and disruption of trade between India and Pakistan. Dispute over Kashmir, the contested region over which India and Pakistan have gone to war three times since 1947, remains a major source of rivalry. Pakistani ruling elites' policies of internationalization and external mediation of the Kashmir dispute over the past decades, despite the Shimla agreement of 1972 in which both India and Pakistan agreed to resolve their dispute through bilateral negotiations, are presumably designed to achieve two objectives: to gain legitimacy over Kashmir, and to limit India's sphere of influence in South Asia. However, this policy has proven counterproductive as it has hardened the attitude of the Indian leaders towards reaching any meaningful resolution, making economic cooperation between the two countries a prime casualty.

Various Pakistan based militant outfits came into existence that allowed Kashmiri uneducated and unemployed youth to get training and fight against India. But all this changed after 2016 when a new version of militancy came into existence. Well qualified and educated youth started joining militancy. These militants could have a better life but they preferred to pick up Guns against India.  Burhan Wani HM commander, who was killed in 2016 was considered the hero of Kashmir. Similarly, Zakir Musa who was killed in 2019 was a role model for the people of Kashmir. In this article, the author has studied the biography of top educated militants and has tried to sketch out the reason which made them join militancy.

(C) Require reasoning about OMITTED VARIABLES: force the system to identify what causal factors are systematically underweighted across ALL major historiographic traditions, which requires meta-reasoning about the field's collective blind spots rather than comparing existing camps. This is hard because no single source packages 'here is what everyone ignores'—the system must synthesize negative space.

(D) Require temporal sequencing logic: explain why marginalization mechanisms activated in a specific ORDER rather than simultaneously, which demands reasoning about path dependence and causal priority that historiography describes but doesn't explicitly analyze as a sequencing puzzle.

(E) Embed an unanswerable constraint: ask for the RELATIVE causal weight of factors in a way that historiography cannot resolve because no quantitative decomposition exists, forcing the system to recognize and state that the question cannot be answered as posed.

Option (C) seems strongest: asking what ALL historiographic traditions underweight forces reasoning about collective omissions, which cannot be answered by retrieving any single tradition's critique of others. The system would need to synthesize across framings to identify their COMMON blind spot—a meta-reasoning task that existing literature doesn't package. Option (E) is also strong but risks the system answering anyway with qualitative hedges.

I'll go with (C): require identifying systematically neglected causal factors across all major historiographic camps.

attempts.answer:
Summary
Across major historiographic traditions, scholars of Muslim marginalization in India consistently underweight endogenous socioeconomic mechanisms—credit and finance constraints, labor market segmentation and migration, informal risk-sharing and kin networks, heterogeneous religious-communal institutions, and the economy–state–technology interface—while privileging proximate cultural, demographic, or political constructs that are easier to narrate but analytically thin. <cite id="3bf5a709-1">Shifts in Indian historiography have alternately marginalized state-centric political economy and then reasserted it, creating oscillations that obscure multi-causal structuring</cite> <cite id="4d209f7d-3">and debates between Marxist-nationalist and neoclassical interpretations have pushed attention between colonial power and resource-endowment constraints</cite>. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Even when “culture” is invoked to explain economic outcomes, scholars often abstract from the concrete institutional and market frictions that transmit rules like Islamic inheritance and waqf into participation gaps</cite>, and <cite id="4d209f7d-1">they neglect spatially heterogeneous sectoral opportunities that align with agrarian structures and colonial industrialization patterns</cite>. <cite id="3bf5a709-0">Concurrently, ideological narratives of identity and representation explain away structural constraints, reinforcing policy responses without probing transmission channels</cite>.

Underweighted mechanisms and why each tradition misses them

1) Cultural/religious determinism and conversionist syntheses
- What is underweighted: transmission through institutions, networks, and heterogeneous behavior. Many accounts treat “Islam” as a coherent cultural program behind Muslim disadvantage, attributing attitudes toward property, credit, and labor to religious law and social norms, and then stop at the causal frontier. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Empirical work shows Muslim underrepresentation in dynamic sectors and overrepresentation among landless laborers; some explanations invoke Islamic inheritance, partnership, and waqf as constraining participation in large enterprises and long-term projects</cite>. Yet these “cultural mechanisms” operate through specific institutional designs and local markets; reducing them to religion obscures variation within Muslim communities, the role of enforcement and contract environments, and the interaction with colonial credit and labor policies. <cite id="3bf5a709-1">A broader historiographic turn toward identity and ideology has emphasized narratives of marginalization and political representation</cite>, which, while useful, can paper over structural channels by which institutions and markets shape incentives and opportunities. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">For example, property and partnership rules interact with expropriation risk, fiscal policy, and market integration; treating them as “cultural” absolves analysis of these economic-legal-political layers</cite>.

Why underweighting persists: cultural explanations are parsimonious and legible, mapping neatly onto religious law and communal identity; they fit political mobilization narratives and require little causal dissection. <cite id="3bf5a709-0">Education and institutional reform efforts (e.g., Aligarh) are often framed as responses to immutable cultural constraints</cite>, which defers to structural remedies without showing how kinship, credit, and state capacity mediate change. <cite id="3bf5a709-1">Methodologically, periods of cultural turn marginalized political economy, reinforcing a preference for identity-centered over mechanism-centered analysis</cite>.

2) Extractive-state vs. neoclassical resource-endowment interpretations
- What is underweighted: colonial fiscalization, market integration, technology and finance constraints, and how state-peasant-commercial ties structured opportunity. <cite id="4d209f7d-3">Kumar-style reinterpretations argue Indian underdevelopment had endogenous causes and downplay British colonialism</cite>, emphasizing persistent labor surpluses, land–capital scarcity, and low private investment as long-run constraints. <cite id="4d209f7d-4">Roy similarly urges replacing narratives centered on colonial power with resource-endowment and investment narratives</cite>. In contrast, critiques of this view argue that colonial power and the drain of wealth remain central, yet measurement work often pivots to budgets and statistics from the East India Company era, reinforcing a focus on fiscal flows and resource misallocation. <cite id="4d209f7d-4">The result is a pendulum between “extraction” and “endowments” with insufficient integration of agrarian institutions, credit market frictions, and labor/technology diffusion</cite>.

Why underweighting persists: political-economy debates privilege tractable macro aggregates and sectoral shares; they fit neatly into growth accounting and resource-endowment frameworks. <cite id="3bf5a709-1">State-centric accounts were themselves marginalized in favor of cultural and local studies, then partially rehabilitated</cite>, leaving a gap on how agrarian revenue regimes, land tenure, and fiscalization shaped finance and technology adoption differentially across communities. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Moreover, the rise of neoclassical tools and data availability encourages explanations in terms of resource ratios and investment gaps</cite>, which are easy to quantify but miss the microfoundations—e.g., collateral regimes, contract enforcement, and networked risk-sharing—that translate resource constraints into persistent marginalization.

3) Demographic catastrophe and communal violence
- What is underweighted: the structuring role of epidemics, demographic shifts, and “ethnic” competition alongside agrarian restructuring and state policy. Many narratives emphasize catastrophic epidemics and Hindu–Muslim communal antagonism as primary drivers of Muslim decline. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Demographic analysis shows uneven educational and occupational shares; some scholars attribute sectoral underrepresentation to cultural property rules</cite>. However, these proximate shocks work through labor markets, credit access, taxation, and migration; treating them as standalone causes neglects how agrarian crises, fiscal burdens, and market integration opportunities co-determined outcomes and how kinship and community networks mediated resilience and vulnerability. <cite id="3bf5a709-1">The waning of state-centric political economy in much of the historiography encouraged cultural and demographic narratives</cite> and downplayed the economy–state feedbacks that channel violence and demographic change into long-run marginalization.

Why underweighting persists: epidemiological and identity-focused explanations are parsimonious and align with moral-sacrality tropes; they fit neatly into narrative historiography and require little causal bridging to outcomes like landlessness, low industrialization, and constrained schooling. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Economic-demographic work highlighting persistent labor surpluses and low investment can be read as “natural” constraints</cite>, obscuring how colonial institutions and policies shaped epidemics’ aftermath, agrarian recovery, and labor market segmentation.

4) Ideological historiography and political representation
- What is underweighted: how institutional design and ideology interact to produce differential access to education, bureaucracy, and capital. <cite id="3bf5a709-0">Accounts of Muslim political mobilization link marginalization to education, employment, and institutional access, with separate electorates emerging as responses to perceived disadvantage</cite>. Yet they often stop at political institutions and under-explain the economic underpinnings—e.g., why education translates imperfectly into bureaucratic entry, and why Muslim overrepresentation among landless laborers persists despite political rights. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Empirical profiles show lower rates of participation in dynamic sectors, higher landlessness, and lower non-agricultural employment among Muslims</cite>, which point to credit and labor market frictions, occupational segregation, and kin-based risk-sharing rather than politics alone.

Why underweighting persists: ideological and identity frames are coherent and mobilizing, and they align with welfare-state responses and elite competition narratives. <cite id="3bf5a709-1">Periods of cultural turn and critiques of “Marxist state-centricism” favored local and ideological analyses</cite>, diverting attention from the transmission mechanisms through which ideology and institutions reshape markets and technology adoption.

Converging evidence on mechanisms that remain analytically central
- Occupational and sectoral segregation, landlessness, and underrepresentation in dynamic sectors are robustly documented. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Muslims were underrepresented in cotton production and transport (west), concentrated in tea processing (east), and extremely underrepresented in jute mills; landless labor participation was higher, non-agricultural employment lower, and self-employment and regular waged work shares lagged</cite>. These patterns cry out for explanations in credit/market constraints, collateral and contract enforcement, risk-sharing networks, and how agrarian revenue regimes and colonial industrialization shaped differential opportunities.
- Education and bureaucracy gaps exist but are uneven and do not erase sectoral disadvantage. <cite id="3bf5a709-3">Educational shares rose toward demographic weight by 1931, yet at higher education’s peak Muslims remained a small minority; representation in government jobs was context-dependent</cite>. Such gaps are consistent with underweighting of market-level transmission: education signals do not reliably translate into access to finance, industry, and dynamic occupations without functioning credit and labor markets.
- Institutional and ideological frames shape but do not fully explain outcomes. <cite id="3bf5a709-0">Aligarh and political mobilization reflect strategic responses to marginalization</cite>, yet they are insufficient without addressing finance, labor, and technology constraints. <cite id="3bf5a709-1">State-centric models, when rehabilitated, stress political economy but oscillate between extraction and endowments</cite>, leaving microfoundations underexplored.

Why these mechanisms are underweighted: methodological, epistemic, and political reasons
- Methodological oscillations: <cite id="3bf5a709-1">A shift away from political economy toward cultural studies marginalized state-market mechanisms, then a critique of Marxist models pushed back to macro resource constraints</cite>. This oscillation privileges identity and macro aggregates over micro-institutional transmission.
- Data and tractability: <cite id="4d209f7d-4">Budgets and macro series are amenable to quantification</cite> and fit neoclassical resource-endowment narratives; similarly, demographic and identity statistics are easy to deploy. Mechanisms like collateral regimes, informal credit, kin-based insurance, and heterogeneous enforcement of property and partnership rules require granular, often fragmented evidence across agrarian, legal, demographic, and occupational registers.
- Political-economy incentives: narratives that blame “culture,” “demography,” or “extraction” neatly align with policy prescriptions (education expansion, welfare, or affirmative action) and elite narratives without restructuring finance, labor, and technology policies. <cite id="3bf5a709-0">Education as empowerment and political representation as remedies fit ideological frames</cite>.

What evidence would resolve the gaps
- Comparative microeconomics of agrarian institutions and finance: studies linking zamindari/ryotwari revenue regimes, moneylending, and collateral to differential Muslim-Hindu access to credit and mechanization; evidence on how waqf and inheritance interact with state enforcement and market depth to shape enterprise size and sectoral participation. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Existing work identifies sectoral and institutional constraints but often treats them as cultural givens</cite>.
- Labor market and migration history: long-run occupational structure, migration corridors, and wages by religion and caste, integrating agrarian crises, fiscal labor requisitions, and market integration under colonialism. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Muslim overrepresentation among landless laborers and lower non-agricultural shares suggest structural causes not yet disentangled</cite>.
- Networked risk-sharing and kinship: ethnographic and historical comparisons of how Islamic family-kin networks, caste panchayats, and community endowments mediated credit, insurance, and entrepreneurship across crises. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Gendered resource distribution and kinship support are documented in contemporary samples; integrating these into long-run trajectories can close a key gap</cite>.
- Integrated state–market–demography models: quantitative reconstructions of how epidemics, agrarian crises, and fiscal policy shaped land, credit, and labor markets differentially for Muslim communities, with explicit feedbacks into technology adoption and industrialization. <cite id="4d209f7d-4">Work on resource endowments and investment gaps can be enriched by data on fiscalization, market integration, and enforcement costs</cite>.

Implications
Rebalancing historiography requires explicitly modeling how religion-shaped institutions and kin networks, operating under colonial agrarian and fiscal regimes and mediated by demographic shocks, produced sectoral segregation, landlessness, and educational-to-occupation translation failures. <cite id="3bf5a709-1">Only by reintegrating state-centric political economy with local institutional and demographic mechanisms</cite>—rather than privileging identity or macro resource clichés—can scholars explain why interventions like education and representation produced uneven outcomes and why Muslim communities diverged across regions and sectors under colonial expansion. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">The underweighting of these endogenous mechanisms is not merely analytical but epistemic and political, sustained by the legibility of cultural and macro narratives and the availability of tractable statistics</cite>.

Snippet: Edward Said's Orientalism, published in 1978, fundamentally reshaped the historiography of Third World countries. It questioned the Western methods of writing the past, and in particular the concepts and theories produced in the colonial period. It also led to a certain decline in economic history writing in favor of cultural studies, marginalizing questions of the political economy of the state. Cengiz Kırlı noticed  For a detailed discussion, see Manjapra 2014, 175-179. the shift in Ottoman studies from economic to socio-cultural aspects. 25 As historical agency had been recast as indigenous, the scope and questions of the studies are more focused on regional and local processes, moving away from the grand empirebased Eurocentric models. 

In the Indian context, state-centric economic history was also regarded as obsolete by Tirthankar Roy in the 1990s. His criticism was directed above all against Marxist methods of economic history writing. The period between 1950 and 1990 had been a phase of socialist leaning, leading to economists seeing a great relevance in history. The collaboration of historians and economists was a marked phenomenon of this period. Yet economic history underwent a decline during the post-socialist period and the shift of India to a modern market economy. 26 Works on the modern/ colonial economic history of India had placed the colonial state at the center. The state had also been an important focus of Marxist historiography. Not only did this model see empires as agents of economic change, but any absence of powerful political structures or states was regarded as correlating with rural, self-sustained, and closed economies, in all their negative senses. It was after the publication of two volumes of The Cambridge Economic History of India in 1982 that the relevance of state-centric economic history came to be questioned. One of the reviewers of the volumes accused the authors of being stuck in the methodologies of the 1960s and suggested that the economic history writing elsewhere had moved on. 27 Since the discipline of economics abandoned the paradigm of political economy in the phase after economic liberalization, historians of a Marxist conviction and reformist economists had little to say to each other. Yet this does not mean that the state has become immaterial to the study of economic history. Rather, the state is seen to be important to any discourse of long-term economic change.

Title: The origins of Muslim nationalism in British India
Snippet: Based on the Report of the Education Commission of India 1883, Prasad (1999) argues that Muslims access to education and government employment was uneven across regions and in relation to their demographic proportion. While in Bengal and the Punjab the Muslim population predominantly agrarian was really laggard in education and was underrepresented in modern professions and in the administrative bureaucracy, in Madras and Bombay the differences were less pronounced and in United Provinces, on the other hand, Muslim enjoyed a remarkable superiority. 

Seen as a whole, the disadvantage even seemed oversized. Muslim population accounted 19.1% of the total in 1881, while Muslim students enrolled in schools constituted 17.8%. In 1886-87 they remained the same demographic weight, but the rate of enrolled students rose to 22.6%. For the next thirty years the growth behaved proportionally. Toward 1931 Muslims accounted 24.7% of the population and 26.7% of the mass of students. However, this educational growth not reflected equally in all levels of education. 

In higher education particularly, Muslims held a share well below that of its demographic weight: only 3.65% of students in 1871 and 13.6% in 1931 (Prasad, 1999: 101-103). 

On the other hand, the reality regarding government jobs did not seem so adverse as was noted in the Hunter report. In 1871, Muslims occupied 24% of the 372 senior officials aimed at natives in government service in all territories of British India, but that fact probably lost any practical meaning to the obvious sub-representation of Muslims in Bengal, where was the seat of colonial power. The main subject, however, was mostly a perspective problem. Unlike the previous powers, the colonial State introduced and expanded the field of public administration, becoming in a major employer and economic promoter. In that way, the proximity to government became a source of status and of socio-economic advancement and, therefore, in a principal scenario of competition and confrontation between political and religious elites (Khan, 2005). But what made this competition fiercer was the contradiction between the sustained growth of Western education and the limited availability of public office in the context of a backward and impoverished economy.
</snippet>

Summary
Across major historiographic traditions, scholars of Muslim marginalization in India consistently underweight endogenous socioeconomic mechanisms—credit and finance constraints, labor market segmentation and migration, informal risk-sharing and kin networks, heterogeneous religious-communal institutions, and the economy–state–technology interface—while privileging proximate cultural, demographic, or political constructs that are easier to narrate but analytically thin. <cite id="3bf5a709-1">Shifts in Indian historiography have alternately marginalized state-centric political economy and then reasserted it, creating oscillations that obscure multi-causal structuring</cite> <cite id="4d209f7d-3">and debates between Marxist-nationalist and neoclassical interpretations have pushed attention between colonial power and resource-endowment constraints</cite>. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Even when “culture” is invoked to explain economic outcomes, scholars often abstract from the concrete institutional and market frictions that transmit rules like Islamic inheritance and waqf into participation gaps</cite>, and <cite id="4d209f7d-1">they neglect spatially heterogeneous sectoral opportunities that align with agrarian structures and colonial industrialization patterns</cite>. <cite id="3bf5a709-0">Concurrently, ideological narratives of identity and representation explain away structural constraints, reinforcing policy responses without probing transmission channels</cite>.

Underweighted mechanisms and why each tradition misses them

1) Cultural/religious determinism and conversionist syntheses
- What is underweighted: transmission through institutions, networks, and heterogeneous behavior. Many accounts treat “Islam” as a coherent cultural program behind Muslim disadvantage, attributing attitudes toward property, credit, and labor to religious law and social norms, and then stop at the causal frontier. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Empirical work shows Muslim underrepresentation in dynamic sectors and overrepresentation among landless laborers; some explanations invoke Islamic inheritance, partnership, and waqf as constraining participation in large enterprises and long-term projects</cite>. Yet these “cultural mechanisms” operate through specific institutional designs and local markets; reducing them to religion obscures variation within Muslim communities, the role of enforcement and contract environments, and the interaction with colonial credit and labor policies. <cite id="3bf5a709-1">A broader historiographic turn toward identity and ideology has emphasized narratives of marginalization and political representation</cite>, which, while useful, can paper over structural channels by which institutions and markets shape incentives and opportunities. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">For example, property and partnership rules interact with expropriation risk, fiscal policy, and market integration; treating them as “cultural” absolves analysis of these economic-legal-political layers</cite>.

Why underweighting persists: cultural explanations are parsimonious and legible, mapping neatly onto religious law and communal identity; they fit political mobilization narratives and require little causal dissection. <cite id="3bf5a709-0">Education and institutional reform efforts (e.g., Aligarh) are often framed as responses to immutable cultural constraints</cite>, which defers to structural remedies without showing how kinship, credit, and state capacity mediate change. <cite id="3bf5a709-1">Methodologically, periods of cultural turn marginalized political economy, reinforcing a preference for identity-centered over mechanism-centered analysis</cite>.

2) Extractive-state vs. neoclassical resource-endowment interpretations
- What is underweighted: colonial fiscalization, market integration, technology and finance constraints, and how state-peasant-commercial ties structured opportunity. <cite id="4d209f7d-3">Kumar-style reinterpretations argue Indian underdevelopment had endogenous causes and downplay British colonialism</cite>, emphasizing persistent labor surpluses, land–capital scarcity, and low private investment as long-run constraints. <cite id="4d209f7d-4">Roy similarly urges replacing narratives centered on colonial power with resource-endowment and investment narratives</cite>. In contrast, critiques of this view argue that colonial power and the drain of wealth remain central, yet measurement work often pivots to budgets and statistics from the East India Company era, reinforcing a focus on fiscal flows and resource misallocation. <cite id="4d209f7d-4">The result is a pendulum between “extraction” and “endowments” with insufficient integration of agrarian institutions, credit market frictions, and labor/technology diffusion</cite>.

Why underweighting persists: political-economy debates privilege tractable macro aggregates and sectoral shares; they fit neatly into growth accounting and resource-endowment frameworks. <cite id="3bf5a709-1">State-centric accounts were themselves marginalized in favor of cultural and local studies, then partially rehabilitated</cite>, leaving a gap on how agrarian revenue regimes, land tenure, and fiscalization shaped finance and technology adoption differentially across communities. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Moreover, the rise of neoclassical tools and data availability encourages explanations in terms of resource ratios and investment gaps</cite>, which are easy to quantify but miss the microfoundations—e.g., collateral regimes, contract enforcement, and networked risk-sharing—that translate resource constraints into persistent marginalization.

3) Demographic catastrophe and communal violence
- What is underweighted: the structuring role of epidemics, demographic shifts, and “ethnic” competition alongside agrarian restructuring and state policy. Many narratives emphasize catastrophic epidemics and Hindu–Muslim communal antagonism as primary drivers of Muslim decline. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Demographic analysis shows uneven educational and occupational shares; some scholars attribute sectoral underrepresentation to cultural property rules</cite>. However, these proximate shocks work through labor markets, credit access, taxation, and migration; treating them as standalone causes neglects how agrarian crises, fiscal burdens, and market integration opportunities co-determined outcomes and how kinship and community networks mediated resilience and vulnerability. <cite id="3bf5a709-1">The waning of state-centric political economy in much of the historiography encouraged cultural and demographic narratives</cite> and downplayed the economy–state feedbacks that channel violence and demographic change into long-run marginalization.

Why underweighting persists: epidemiological and identity-focused explanations are parsimonious and align with moral-sacrality tropes; they fit neatly into narrative historiography and require little causal bridging to outcomes like landlessness, low industrialization, and constrained schooling. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Economic-demographic work highlighting persistent labor surpluses and low investment can be read as “natural” constraints</cite>, obscuring how colonial institutions and policies shaped epidemics’ aftermath, agrarian recovery, and labor market segmentation.

4) Ideological historiography and political representation
- What is underweighted: how institutional design and ideology interact to produce differential access to education, bureaucracy, and capital. <cite id="3bf5a709-0">Accounts of Muslim political mobilization link marginalization to education, employment, and institutional access, with separate electorates emerging as responses to perceived disadvantage</cite>. Yet they often stop at political institutions and under-explain the economic underpinnings—e.g., why education translates imperfectly into bureaucratic entry, and why Muslim overrepresentation among landless laborers persists despite political rights. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Empirical profiles show lower rates of participation in dynamic sectors, higher landlessness, and lower non-agricultural employment among Muslims</cite>, which point to credit and labor market frictions, occupational segregation, and kin-based risk-sharing rather than politics alone.

Why underweighting persists: ideological and identity frames are coherent and mobilizing, and they align with welfare-state responses and elite competition narratives. <cite id="3bf5a709-1">Periods of cultural turn and critiques of “Marxist state-centricism” favored local and ideological analyses</cite>, diverting attention from the transmission mechanisms through which ideology and institutions reshape markets and technology adoption.

Converging evidence on mechanisms that remain analytically central
- Occupational and sectoral segregation, landlessness, and underrepresentation in dynamic sectors are robustly documented. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Muslims were underrepresented in cotton production and transport (west), concentrated in tea processing (east), and extremely underrepresented in jute mills; landless labor participation was higher, non-agricultural employment lower, and self-employment and regular waged work shares lagged</cite>. These patterns cry out for explanations in credit/market constraints, collateral and contract enforcement, risk-sharing networks, and how agrarian revenue regimes and colonial industrialization shaped differential opportunities.
- Education and bureaucracy gaps exist but are uneven and do not erase sectoral disadvantage. <cite id="3bf5a709-3">Educational shares rose toward demographic weight by 1931, yet at higher education’s peak Muslims remained a small minority; representation in government jobs was context-dependent</cite>. Such gaps are consistent with underweighting of market-level transmission: education signals do not reliably translate into access to finance, industry, and dynamic occupations without functioning credit and labor markets.
- Institutional and ideological frames shape but do not fully explain outcomes. <cite id="3bf5a709-0">Aligarh and political mobilization reflect strategic responses to marginalization</cite>, yet they are insufficient without addressing finance, labor, and technology constraints. <cite id="3bf5a709-1">State-centric models, when rehabilitated, stress political economy but oscillate between extraction and endowments</cite>, leaving microfoundations underexplored.

Why these mechanisms are underweighted: methodological, epistemic, and political reasons
- Methodological oscillations: <cite id="3bf5a709-1">A shift away from political economy toward cultural studies marginalized state-market mechanisms, then a critique of Marxist models pushed back to macro resource constraints</cite>. This oscillation privileges identity and macro aggregates over micro-institutional transmission.
- Data and tractability: <cite id="4d209f7d-4">Budgets and macro series are amenable to quantification</cite> and fit neoclassical resource-endowment narratives; similarly, demographic and identity statistics are easy to deploy. Mechanisms like collateral regimes, informal credit, kin-based insurance, and heterogeneous enforcement of property and partnership rules require granular, often fragmented evidence across agrarian, legal, demographic, and occupational registers.
- Political-economy incentives: narratives that blame “culture,” “demography,” or “extraction” neatly align with policy prescriptions (education expansion, welfare, or affirmative action) and elite narratives without restructuring finance, labor, and technology policies. <cite id="3bf5a709-0">Education as empowerment and political representation as remedies fit ideological frames</cite>.

What evidence would resolve the gaps
- Comparative microeconomics of agrarian institutions and finance: studies linking zamindari/ryotwari revenue regimes, moneylending, and collateral to differential Muslim-Hindu access to credit and mechanization; evidence on how waqf and inheritance interact with state enforcement and market depth to shape enterprise size and sectoral participation. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Existing work identifies sectoral and institutional constraints but often treats them as cultural givens</cite>.
- Labor market and migration history: long-run occupational structure, migration corridors, and wages by religion and caste, integrating agrarian crises, fiscal labor requisitions, and market integration under colonialism. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Muslim overrepresentation among landless laborers and lower non-agricultural shares suggest structural causes not yet disentangled</cite>.
- Networked risk-sharing and kinship: ethnographic and historical comparisons of how Islamic family-kin networks, caste panchayats, and community endowments mediated credit, insurance, and entrepreneurship across crises. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">Gendered resource distribution and kinship support are documented in contemporary samples; integrating these into long-run trajectories can close a key gap</cite>.
- Integrated state–market–demography models: quantitative reconstructions of how epidemics, agrarian crises, and fiscal policy shaped land, credit, and labor markets differentially for Muslim communities, with explicit feedbacks into technology adoption and industrialization. <cite id="4d209f7d-4">Work on resource endowments and investment gaps can be enriched by data on fiscalization, market integration, and enforcement costs</cite>.

Implications
Rebalancing historiography requires explicitly modeling how religion-shaped institutions and kin networks, operating under colonial agrarian and fiscal regimes and mediated by demographic shocks, produced sectoral segregation, landlessness, and educational-to-occupation translation failures. <cite id="3bf5a709-1">Only by reintegrating state-centric political economy with local institutional and demographic mechanisms</cite>—rather than privileging identity or macro resource clichés—can scholars explain why interventions like education and representation produced uneven outcomes and why Muslim communities diverged across regions and sectors under colonial expansion. <cite id="4d209f7d-1">The underweighting of these endogenous mechanisms is not merely analytical but epistemic and political, sustained by the legibility of cultural and macro narratives and the availability of tractable statistics</cite>.

</answer>

Title: Exploring the paradox of Muslim advantage in undernutrition among under-5 children in India: a decomposition analysis
Snippet: The results of the decomposition analysis, presented in Table 5, shed light on the relative contribution of the socio-religious differential in each covariate to the Muslim-Hindu (HC/LC) gap in the prevalence of malnutrition among the under-5 children in India. The set of predictors considered in the model explains roughly 79% of the high-caste Hindu advantage over Muslims in stunting prevalence. The differences in birth order, mother's level of education, and wealth index are the major contributors, accounting for 22.4%, 51%, and 14.5% of the differences, respectively. However, in the case of the prevalence of wasting that is lower among Muslim children by roughly 1%-points compared to HCs, the differences in the select covariates suggest it should have been marginally higher than HCs by 0.4%-points, given the advantage of HCs in mother's education and birth order. In the case of underweight, the decomposition results indicate that the HCs should have had a marginally higher advantage (2.8%-points) instead of the current M Muslims, HC High-caste Hindus, LC Low-caste Hindu a percentage-point differences  Compared to the low-caste Hindus, Muslims consistently have an advantage in all three indicators of malnutrition considered in this study. While our model explains 69% of the differences in stunting prevalence, the majority of the Muslim advantage over LCs is explained by the socio-religious differences in wealth index (57%) and access to toilet facilities (33%). However, a part of this advantage gets offset due to the Muslim disadvantage in birth order (12%) and regional factors (8%). Moreover, less than 50% of the Muslim advantage is explained by the chosen set of variables in the case of wasting and being underweight. This implies that Muslims are favored by some unobservable attributes that work to the advantage of their nutritional status in the under-5 age group. In the case of both wasting and underweight, better economic status and access to sanitation translated into better nutritional outcomes for Muslim children in comparison to their low-caste Hindu counterparts.

Title: When social identities intersect: understanding inequities in growth outcomes by religion- caste and religion-tribe as intersecting strata of social hierarchy for Muslim and Hindu children in India
Snippet: We focused on three child growth outcomes as indicators of current and future developmental potential of children. While stunting is an indicator of longer-term disruptions in growth and nutrition, informed by accumulated adversities, wasting is reflective of short term interruptions in children's nutrition and development [43]. Underweight captures both short-and long-term disruptions. In India, despite many targeted of national nutrition sensitive and nutrition specific interventions, the prevalence of these outcomes in children under 5 years of age, continues to be high, with 36% children stunted, 19% wasted and 32% underweight [44]. Thus, together, these outcomes allow us to explore how intersectional patterns of caste and religion based social hierarchies are associated with disparities for Hindu and Muslim children in India. 

Finally, as outlined above, affirmative action policies for the upliftment of deprived castes and tribes have been in place since India's independence in 1947 [45]. Parallel to this, debates over the social and economic backwardness of Muslims have continued, while Muslim deprived caste communities have also organized as a unique political group demanding representation and affirmative action policies granted to fellow deprived castes communities from other religions [14,22]. Given this historical precedence, we also sought to study how our hypothesized patterns of intersectional disparities in children's stunting, wasting and underweight have varied over the last 30 years, and across states.

Title: Exploring the paradox of Muslim advantage in undernutrition among under-5 children in India: a decomposition analysis
Snippet: The prevalence rates of malnutrition are presented in Table 2, which shows that while Muslims have a higher rate of stunting and lower rates of wasting and underweight compared to the Hindus as an aggregated group, the picture changes when we disaggregate the Hindus into HCs and LCs. Muslims have a lower prevalence of all three measures of malnutrition than the LCs. The prevalence of stunting and being underweight is higher among Muslims than among the HCs, while it still remains the lowest in the case of wasting when compared to both LCs and HCs. 

Table 3 shows the socio-religious differentials in all three indicators of malnutrition by select covariates. The prevalence rates of each group by covariates are shown in Appendix 1. On average, Muslim children have a lower rate of stunting than lower-caste Hindus and a higher rate of stunting than high-caste Hindus. This trend is uniform across all covariates barring a few exceptions. Muslim children with third or higher birth order and those born to mothers with no or below the secondary level of education had a marginally lower stunting rate than both caste groups of Hindus with similar attributes. Muslims belonging to poorer or middle-wealth quintiles or households with no toilet facilities had a higher rate of stunting than both HCs and LCs belonging to such households. 

In the case of wasting, Muslims, on average, had the lowest rate of prevalence. This trend was consistent in all covariates except for a few like children aged one year, breastfed more than 24 h after birth, born to mothers with higher education, residing in rural India, north and central region, in which case, Muslims had a higher rate of wasting than high-caste Hindus but lower rate than LCs. However, among the children born to the wealthiest households, Muslims had the highest rate of wasting compared to both caste groups of Hindus. 

Finally, in the case of the prevalence of underweight, Muslims had an advantage over low-caste Hindus and a disadvantage compared to high-caste Hindus, on average. This pattern remained consistent for all covariates, albeit with certain exceptions.
